																$389.99 at  B&H										 | 
																$634.97 at  Amazon						
					
The LaCie Rugged SSD4 is a portable USB4 drive that combines fast transfers with LaCie’s familiar orange protective sleeve. We liked its strong Mac performance, recording approximately 2,975MB/s for reading and 3,300MB/s for writing – comfortably sufficient for large file transfers and demanding everyday work. Its IP54 rating protects against dust and splashes, while LaCie also specifies resistance to three-meter drops and one-tonne crushing pressure. A three-year warranty with Rescue Data Recovery Services strengthens its appeal for people working away from the office. Our main design complaint was the easily misplaced removable USB port cover. However, reported discontinuation and uncertain stock now undermine its position as a leading recommendation. Consider remaining stock only when the price compares favorably with current USB4 alternatives offering similar performance and protection.






$129.99 at  LaCie						
					





The LaCie Portable SSD is a small USB-C drive aimed at people who want straightforward additional storage without a bulky enclosure. We liked its attractive silver design, solid construction, and exceptionally light, pocketable form. Its USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection offers sufficient performance for everyday transfers, photo libraries, and backups, although it was an average performer within its class rather than a speed leader. Reviewed capacities ranged from 500GB to 2TB, making it suitable for carrying a working collection of documents and media. Its appeal was always the combination of portability, simplicity, and style. However, retailers now identify reviewed models as discontinued or end of life. We would choose a more readily available alternative unless remaining stock comes with a compelling discount and a trustworthy seller.


		
$279.99 at  Sandisk										 | 
																$654.89 at  Newegg US										 | 
																$999.99 at  Walmart						
					
The SanDisk Extreme Pro with USB4 is a rugged portable SSD available in 2TB and 4TB capacities. We liked its strong performance on Macs, with our Thunderbolt 4 MacBook Pro recording approximately 3,400MB/s for both reading and writing. Its forged aluminum body and protective silicone covering give it a reassuringly sturdy feel, supported by IP65 dust and water resistance and a five-year warranty. The main drawback is size: it is noticeably larger and heavier than many portable competitors. SanDisk now offers a newer Extreme Pro V3, so this older model makes more sense as a discounted alternative than the default recommendation. Check the model number carefully: SDSSDE82 identifies this version. 






$94.99 at  Seagate										 | 
																$109.99 at  Walmart						
					
The Seagate One Touch SSD is a compact portable drive designed for straightforward backups and everyday file transfers. We liked its light, sturdy construction and the inclusion of both USB-C and USB-A cables, making it convenient to use across different computers. The reviewed model offered 500GB, 1TB, and 2TB capacities, with enough performance for documents, photos, and media libraries. Seagate’s Toolkit software adds folder synchronization. The absence of hardware encryption is a limitation for people carrying sensitive files. It could still be worth buying at a competitive price; be careful to distinguish the faster STKG generation from older STJE models.






$59.99 at  Western Digital										 | 
																$208.62 at  Amazon										 | 
																$379.99 at  Walmart						
					
The WD My Passport SSD is a lightweight USB-C drive intended for everyday portable storage, with hardware encryption among its attractions. We liked its slim design and useful performance when connected to a suitable USB 3.2 Gen 2 port. Compatibility with USB-A connections also makes it practical for people moving files between newer and older computers. However, the unusually short cable can be inconvenient. It remains worth comparing when discounted, particularly if encrypted portable storage is your priority.






$84.99 at  Lacie										 | 
																$127.30 at  Amazon						
					
The LaCie Rugged Mini SSD is a portable drive wrapped in the company’s distinctive orange protective sleeve. We liked its sturdy construction, pocketable design, and three-year warranty with Rescue Data Recovery Services. It provides a useful way to carry backups or project files when traveling, with reviewed capacities extending to 4TB. However, its USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 interface is a significant consideration for Mac buyers: the Macs used in our testing could not achieve its advertised 2,000MB/s performance. We recorded approximately 900MB/s for writing and 970MB/s for reading, which remains sufficient for routine backups. It is still worth considering at a competitive price, particularly if its protective design and recovery service matter more than maximum transfer speeds.






$209.99 at  Adorama										 | 
																$209.99 at  B&H						
					
The Lexar Armor 700 is a rugged portable SSD aimed at photographers, filmmakers, and anyone carrying important files outdoors. We liked its slim design, grippy protective covering, and IP66 rating for resistance to dust and powerful water jets. Its construction makes it an appealing travel companion, while encryption software provides another useful feature for sensitive files. The important limitation for Mac buyers is its USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 interface: without support for that connection standard, a Mac cannot deliver the drive’s advertised maximum performance. It remains fast enough for ordinary backups, but USB4 alternatives are better suited to buyers prioritizing speed. A substantial discount could still make it an attractive purchase for travel.






$281.05 at  Amazon						
					
The Verbatim TurboMetal SSD is a portable USB4 drive with a rounded metal enclosure and a temperature-controlled cooling fan. We liked its attractive construction, quiet fan, and good transfer speeds. Testing on an M3 MacBook Air produced approximately 2,664MB/s for writing and 3,123MB/s for reading, with stronger results on an M4 Max Mac Studio. Reviewed capacities ranged from 1TB to 4TB. However, sustained testing exposed temporary speed reductions as the drive warmed up, before cooling restored performance. Mac users should also reformat the drive appropriately, and the included software is Windows-only. Other USB4 options offer a clearer combination of performance and convenience. It remains a reasonable alternative when discounted, particularly for everyday transfers that do not involve continuously writing large amounts of data.






The Adata SE920 is a high-performance portable USB4 SSD designed for demanding work such as photo and video editing. We liked its fast, consistent transfers and effective cooling system, which combines a metal enclosure with a small fan. Pressing the housing expands it and activates the fan, giving users additional cooling during sustained activity. Our testing recorded approximately 2,992MB/s for writing and 3,161MB/s for reading, with stable performance over longer periods. Its setup is less convenient for Mac users because it arrives formatted as NTFS and includes Windows-focused backup software, although reformatting with Disk Utility is straightforward. It remains worth considering if its price undercuts comparable USB4 models and you are comfortable handling the initial setup yourself.






$49.99 at  Western Digital										 | 
																$485.31 at  Amazon						
					
The SanDisk Professional Pro-Blade system is modular storage designed for creative workflows spanning location work and the studio. We liked the flexibility of its removable SSD Mag modules, which can move between a portable Transport enclosure and the desktop Station. The modules are designed to withstand rough handling, and the Station accommodates four of them for a larger storage setup. This makes the system useful for teams exchanging footage or maintaining separate project drives. However, a Mag cannot connect directly to your Mac, so the required enclosure adds cost and complexity. The Transport’s USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 connection also limits performance on Macs without that interface. Most readers will find a conventional portable SSD simpler and more economical.






$299.99 at  Amazon										 | 
																$305.19 at  Newegg US										 | 
																$346.1 at  Walmart						
					
The Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 SSD Dock combines desktop expansion with built-in solid-state storage. We liked the convenience of adding fast storage alongside an extensive selection of connections, including Thunderbolt 5, 2.5Gb Ethernet, and memory card readers. It can also provide up to 140W of charging power to a compatible laptop, making it an appealing foundation for a MacBook workstation. The SSD impressed in our testing, delivering approximately 5,331MB/s for writing and 5,822MB/s for reading in AJA’s 4K test. However, this is a premium docking station rather than a straightforward portable drive, and its cost makes most sense when you need the extra connections. It serves a different purpose to the other SSDs in this roundup, although it remains attractive for an equipped desktop workspace.






$79.99 at  B & H Photo						
					
The Seagate Ultra Compact SSD combines the convenience of a USB thumb drive with the performance of a portable SSD. We liked its small size, sturdy housing, and cable-free connection, making it easy to carry files without packing additional accessories. Our Mac testing recorded approximately 943MB/s for writing and 930MB/s for reading, comfortably sufficient for everyday transfers and suitable video recording tasks. Its IP54 rating provides protection against dust and splashes, while Seagate specifies resistance to three-meter drops. However, the short USB-C connector may not reach an iPhone’s port through some protective cases. It remains an appealing alternative for buyers who want compact USB-C storage and value its protective construction.






How we test Mac SSDs
Our reviews combine benchmark results with hands-on use to assess transfer performance, portability, construction and everyday convenience. We identify the test platform where relevant, including results from our colleagues at PCWorld. Performance varies with the computer, connection and workload, so we distinguish measured results from manufacturers’ advertised speeds. We also assess practical details such as cables, power requirements, security features and warranty coverage.
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld has been testing Mac hardware for decades. Our recommendations draw on hands-on reviews from our team and colleagues across Foundry, with particular attention to Mac compatibility, useful performance and value.
How to choose an SSD: Buying advice
You’ve read our recommendations of the best SSDs for Mac owners on the market right now. But how did we reach these decisions, and what general advice should you follow when selecting the best SSD for your needs?
SSDs vs hard drives
Hard drives generally offer more storage for your money, making them a good choice for large backups where capacity matters more than speed. SSDs typically cost more per gigabyte, but provide faster transfers and are usually smaller and lighter. They also have no moving parts, making them better suited to carrying alongside a MacBook.
If you decide in favor of hard drives, see our roundup of the best Mac hard drives.
Which SSD connection should you choose?
For an external SSD, prioritize the connection supported by both the drive and your Mac. A fast SSD can’t deliver its full performance through a slower port or cable. Everyday backups rarely need the fastest connection, while large video projects and frequent transfers can justify paying for USB4 or Thunderbolt.
USB-C doesn’t tell you the speed
USB-C describes the connector’s shape, rather than its transfer speed. Drives with identical-looking USB-C connectors can use different USB or Thunderbolt standards and offer very different performance.
The table below compares connection bandwidth, rather than guaranteed file-transfer speeds.


ConnectionMaximum connection bandwidthBest suited to

USB 3.2 Gen 15GbpsRoutine backups and everyday storage
USB 3.2 Gen 210GbpsGeneral transfers, backups and photo libraries
USB 3.2 Gen 2×220GbpsCompatible computers; limited performance on many Macs
USB4 at 40Gbps / Thunderbolt 3 or 440GbpsLarge transfers and demanding photo or video work
Thunderbolt 580Gbps for storageMaximum performance on compatible Macs

 



USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 deserves particular attention. Macs that support USB transfers at only 10Gbps won’t deliver a Gen 2×2 drive’s advertised 20Gbps performance. A Thunderbolt port doesn’t automatically remove that limitation.
To get the most from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD, you need a Thunderbolt 5-equipped Mac. Its higher storage bandwidth can support much faster transfers, but connecting a slower USB drive to that port won’t increase the drive’s own maximum speed.
What about SATA and NVMe?
SATA and NVMe describe the storage technology inside a drive, rather than the external connection to your Mac. SATA SSDs typically top out at around 550MB/s, while NVMe SSDs use PCIe and can achieve substantially higher speeds.
However, an external enclosure’s connection can become the bottleneck. An NVMe SSD capable of several gigabytes per second internally won’t achieve those speeds through a 10Gbps USB connection.
For a ready-made external SSD, our measured performance is more useful than its internal PCIe generation alone. If you’re assembling your own external drive, choose an enclosure that supports your SSD’s type and a connection your Mac can exploit.
Match the drive, port and cable
Use a cable rated for the drive’s connection standard. If you connect through a hub or dock, its supported speeds and shared bandwidth also matter.
Actual transfers depend on file sizes, sustained-write performance and the storage at the other end. Choose a drive based on its tested performance in the kind of work you do, rather than connection bandwidth alone.
How much SSD storage do you need?
Choosing the right external SSD capacity depends on what you plan to store. Capacities vary by model, with several recommendations here extending to 8TB. Allow enough space for your existing files and room for your collection to grow, especially if you work with photos or video.
These starting points can help:
500GB–1TB: Everyday documents, smaller photo collections and transferring files between devices.
1TB–2TB: Larger photo libraries, individual video projects and more substantial everyday storage.
4TB–8TB: Extensive photo and video collections, multiple large projects or substantial backup archives.
For backups, consider how much data you need to protect and allow additional space for older versions you may want to recover. For a working drive, consider the size of your projects and how many you need to keep available at once. A smaller SSD may suffice if you regularly move completed projects to separate storage.
Avoid buying a drive that your files will fill immediately. Leaving free space provides room to grow and can help maintain performance, although the effect of filling a drive varies by model and workload.
Compare the price per terabyte across capacities. Larger models sometimes offer better value, but the highest capacity isn’t automatically the best deal. Balance the price with the space you’ll realistically use.
How portable does your SSD need to be?
Most external SSDs are small enough to carry in a laptop bag, but size, weight and cable design affect convenience. A compact, lightweight drive suits frequent travel, while built-in connectors eliminate a separate cable but may obstruct an adjacent port.
For outdoor use, look for a sturdy enclosure and a stated IP rating for dust and water resistance. Water resistance doesn’t necessarily mean a drive can withstand immersion.
Also consider power requirements. Most portable SSDs draw power from your Mac, but the SanDisk Desk Drive requires mains power, making it better suited to a permanent desk setup.
Shock-proof and rugged?
Other features to look out for include IP-ratings for weather protection and password protection for your important files.
SSDs are more durable than hard drives. They have no moving parts, and are less vulnerable to knocks and movement than mechanical hard drives while writing data. While modern hard drives have some level of shock protection, it’s still a big issue.
However, SSDs can still suffer physical damage or fail, so handle them carefully and keep another copy of important files.
Some portable SSDs even offer water resistance. You can also get ruggedization in a specialized drive enclosure, if you choose to go down the 2.5in drive route.
This is a huge portability benefit. But if they are sat still all day, are SSDs more reliable than HDDs? Hard drives tend to fail mechanically. For example, the motor that spins the platters might burn out. SSDs’ memory cells age, which can lead to failure. Both kinds require specialist recovery. As ever, 
back up important data.
However, for our purposes, as people who occasionally have to fling drives in rucksacks and plug them in while sat in an airplane seat, SSDs are the clear winner.
Software
Just remember to check that any apps provided by the manufacturer work with Macs as well as Windows PCs.

title: Apple will reportedly eliminate the Action button in 2027
content:
Macworld





Do you use the Action Button? With the iPhone 15 Pro and every model after, Apple replaced the mute switch (an iPhone staple since the original) with a programmable button.
It doesn’t seem to be very popular. Most users seem to just leave it as a Mute toggle, and even then you see people just using the volume buttons to quiet their iPhone.
A new leak from popular Weibo account Instant Digital claims that Apple is going to get rid of it starting with the phones coming in the second half of 2027. Other iPhone models would lose the button over time, as their physical enclosures are updated.
Apple will combine the function of the Action button with the Camera button, according to the leak. You press the Camera button to launch the camera (or press the shutter if you have a camera app/mode open) and you long-press the button to perform the Action button function.
A long-press of the Action button used to invoke Visual Intelligence. When that feature went underutilized, Apple added it as a new “Siri” mode in the Camera app. Now, a long-press on the Camera button opens the Camera app to the Siri mode, which could be confusing as it looks very close to just opening the camera in general. The rumored change would eliminate that issue by taking away the current Camera > Siri default action for holding down the Action button, and replacing it the Mute toggle or other action of your choosing.

title: Apple Pay Ad Features Martial Arts Convenience Store Food Fight
content:
Apple today shared a humorous new Apple Pay ad that promotes the benefit of the on-device payment option over cash and physical cards.



The spot features a martial-arts-style food fight where a man runs into a convenience store to grab a weapon. He's followed by the other combatants, and everyone involved grabs a different food or beverage to fight with.

Face ID verification is required. The protagonist wins when he purchases a swordfish, causing his opponents to flee.
Apple Pay is a fast, easy, and secure way to pay with iPhone. No digging for cards. Just double-click the side button, glance at your iPhone to authenticate with Face ID, then hold it near the reader. A ding confirms your payment. The built-in security of iPhone makes paying with Apple Pay more secure than using a physical credit or debit card. Use it anywhere you see a contactless payment symbol — from big box retailers to your local corner market.

‌Apple Pay‌ is a popular contactless payment option available in many countries around the world. It works in retail shops on iPhone and Apple Watch. ‌Apple Pay‌ also works in apps and on the web, and on iPad and Mac for online purchases.

title: Best MacBook for 2026: Air vs Pro vs Neo compared
content:
Macworld





Apple sells several MacBook models across different sizes, prices, and performance levels, so choosing the right one depends on your budget, the type of work you do, and how much power you actually need.
In this in-depth guide, we explain which MacBook is best for different users, compare the latest MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and the MacBook Pro models (with and without touchscreen), and help you decide how much RAM and how much storage you really need.
Choosing a MacBook Pro now involves two decisions: how much processing power you need, and which display you want. The entry-level 14-inch model uses the M6 chip, while more demanding users can choose M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations with either a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display or a PROLED XDR OLED touchscreen.
For most people, the MacBook Air remains our recommended starting point. If you need a Pro, choose the chip, memory and storage around your workload, then consider whether the touchscreen model’s OLED display and lighter design justify the extra cost. In this article, we’ll help you decide whether a MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, or MacBook Neo is the best fit for your needs.


Which MacBook is right for you?
In 2026, Apple’s laptop lineup spans five main choices: the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, the mainstream MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro, the high-performance M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro and the touchscreen versions of those MacBook Pro models.
Best for basic use and tight budgets: MacBook Neo is ideal for students, casual browsing, streaming, and light productivity at the lowest entry price.
Best for most people: MacBook Air (M5)  offers the best mix of portability, battery life, silent operation, and everyday performance.
Best for those who want a superior display and extra ports: The MacBook Pro (M6) offers professional-grade features without the extreme power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. 
Best for professionals and power users: MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max) is best for demanding workflows such as 4K video editing, 3D work, heavy multitasking, and software development.
Best for high-end creative professionals: Suited to those who work extensively on their laptop’s built-in display and need direct touch interaction. 
Use the table below to quickly find the MacBook that best suit your needs, or read on for more detailed guide to help you choose the best MacBook for your specific needs.

MacBook Pro (M6)A better display, more ports, and sustained performance.14.2-inch$1,999Amazon / Apple

Touchscreen MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max)High-end creative professionals who need OLED and touch interaction.14.2-inch or 16.3-inch$2,899 / $4,499 Amazon / Apple

If you’re also wondering whether it’s the right time to buy, read our guide: Should you buy the MacBook Air now or wait?
Which MacBook is best in 2026
Below we recommend the best MacBooks for various users, from students and every day users, to professionals, creatives and content creators. We also compare MacBook Air or MacBook Pro for those wondering which model to buy. Below this section you can find general advice about choosing the best specs, including screen size, when purchasing a new Mac.

The MacBook Air (M5) is the best MacBook for most buyers because it offers the strongest balance of price, portability, battery life, and performance.
The 13-inch MacBook Air is light, quiet, fast enough for everyday work, and easier to recommend than any other Mac laptop. The latest version, updated in March 2026, keeps the same winning formula while improving storage and connectivity. There is also a 15-inch version for anyone who wants a larger screen. 
What’s new
The latest MacBook Air features the M5 chip, base storage is 512GB, and it supports newer wireless standards including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Why we recommend the MacBook Air
Excellent balance of performance and portability
Silent fanless design
Long battery life
Strong everyday performance for work, school, and travel
Now ships with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage as standard
Sizes
The MacBook Air comes in two sizes:
13-inch MacBook Air, 13.6-inch screen: Best for portability
15-inch MacBook Air, 15.3-inch screen: Better for multitasking and split-screen work
Display
As you can see from the above measurements, the display, when measured diagonally is a little larger than the standard naming would suggest. As a result the 13-inch MacBook Air display is actually larger than that on the 13-inch MacBook Neo, discussed below. The MacBook Air uses a bright Liquid Retina display, but it still lacks the 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and HDR capabilities found on MacBook Pro models.
Performance
The M5 chip in the MacBook Air is fast enough for office work, school tasks, web apps, multitasking, and light creative work. Because the Air has no fan, though, performance can dip during long video exports or other sustained heavy workloads so that the temperature remains optimal.
Battery life
Battery life is excellent, making the Air a great choice for anyone who works away from a desk. It offers more battery life than the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, but falls short of the 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Other specs
You get MagSafe 3 for charging and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The MacBook Air also supports up to two external displays. (Older M1 and M2 models were limited to one external monitor). 
16GB RAM to 32GB RAM
From 512GB to 4TB SSD
Price
Apple put MacBook Air prices up by $200 in June 2026. 
13-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,299/£1,299
15-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,499/£1,499
What to know before buying
The Air’s biggest limitation is sustained performance. It is quick for most tasks, but it is not the right machine for users who regularly push their system for long periods. The MacBook Air is likely to soon adopt the M6 chip as used in the entry-level MacBook Pro, Mac mini and iMac.

The MacBook Neo is the cheapest way to buy a Mac laptop in 2026. Now starting at $699 (which is unfortunately $100 more than it was when Apple launched it in March), it is aimed at students, first-time Mac buyers, and casual users who mainly browse the web, stream video, join video calls, and work in basic apps.
Despite its lower price, it still looks and feels like a MacBook, with an all-aluminum design and a lightweight chassis.
Who is MacBook Neo for?
The MacBook Neo is best for people whose computing needs are simple: web browsing, email, documents, streaming, and schoolwork.
Why we recommend MacBook Neo
Lowest price in the lineup
Light and portable
Quiet fanless design
Good battery life
Fast enough for basic everyday use
Sizes
The MacBook Neo comes in just one size:
13-inch MacBook Neo, 13-inch screen
Display 
Like the MacBook Air the MacBook Neo offers a Liquid Retina display with max 500 nits brightness, but that’s where the similarities end. The display is slightly smaller than the display on the 13-inch MacBook Air, offering 2,408 by 1,506 pixels compared to 2,560 by 1,664 pixels. It also lacks the wide color P3 and True Tone technology of the other MacBooks, offering only sRGB color. 
Performance 
The MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip – the same processor first introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro. While it is a mobile-class chip, its performance is optimized for a laptop environment, offering a highly responsive experience for everyday productivity. In our tests it proved faster than the M3 in single-core, while equal to the M1 when it came to multi-core performance and graphics. 
Battery life 
The MacBook Neo should comfortably last a working day of general productivity. In our video-loop battery test, with screen brightness set to 150 nits, it lasted 13 hours and 15 minutes. Apple advertises up to 16 hours of video streaming or 11 hours of wireless web browsing. More demanding tasks will drain the battery faster.
Other specs
You get two USB-C ports, but these are not identical in capability, one being USB 3 and the other USB 2. See MacBook Neo ports explained. The MacBook Neo only supports one external display with a resolution of up to 4K at 60Hz.
8GB RAM

What to know before buying
The Neo makes several trade-offs to achieve its low price, including the absence of a backlit keyboard, a limited selection of ports, and no Touch ID on the base model. It also features a lower-quality display compared to the Air and Pro, offers less memory with a maximum of 8GB RAM, and delivers lower sustained performance than M-series MacBooks. For many buyers, the 512GB, $799 model represents better value, as it includes Touch ID and additional storage.
Alternatives
The MacBook Neo is the best budget MacBook, but it is best suited to light workloads. If you can spend more, the MacBook Air remains the better long-term buy for most people.
Another option, if a low price is your top priority, is a refurbished MacBook. Look out for clearance deals on older Apple silicon MacBooks, but avoid the older Intel-based models. See: MacBook Pro deals and MacBook Air deals.

The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro is worth considering if you want more features than the MacBook Air offers without paying for an M5 Pro or M5 Max. Its active cooling suits longer workloads, while its HDR display and additional ports are useful for creative work.
Why we recommend the M6 MacBook Pro
Active cooling for sustained workloads
ProMotion and HDR display

Sizes
The M6 model comes in one size: a 14.2-inch screen.
Display
The non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display uses mini-LED technology, with up to 1,600 nits peak HDR brightness and adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz.
Performance
The M6 has a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU. Choose it for everyday work and creative projects; consider M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations when you need greater graphics or memory capacity.
Battery life
Apple rates it for up to 24 hours of video streaming or 16 hours of wireless web browsing. Actual endurance depends on your workload.

MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
The M5 MacBook Air and M6 MacBook Pro are different in some significant ways.

Foundry




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work and light creative projects in a thin, light, silent design. Choose the MacBook Pro if you regularly run demanding workloads or will benefit from its better display and additional ports.
The closest comparison is between the M5 MacBook Air and 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. For more demanding professional work, the MacBook Pro also offers M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with a choice of non-touchscreen or PROLED XDR touchscreen displays.
Performance: Do you need a MacBook Pro?
The M5 MacBook Air is well suited to web browsing, office apps, studying, photo editing, and occasional video projects. Using creative software doesn’t automatically mean you need a Pro: the size of your projects and how frequently you run demanding tasks matter more.
The M6 MacBook Pro combines a newer chip generation with active cooling. Its fans help it sustain performance during lengthy video exports, code compilation, and other intensive tasks. The Air’s fanless design keeps it completely silent, but performance can fall during prolonged heavy workloads.
If these demanding tasks make up much of your working day, consider an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. These offer greater processing, graphics, and memory capacity than the standard M6 model. A newer chip generation doesn’t automatically make the M6 the more powerful choice.
Display and ports: What does the Pro add?
The MacBook Air’s Liquid Retina display is suitable for everyday work, with 500 nits brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. You can choose a 13-inch model for portability or a 15-inch model for more workspace.
The M6 MacBook Pro’s 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display adds mini-LED technology, deeper contrast, brighter HDR highlights, and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. These features are particularly useful for viewing and editing HDR content, although you don’t need to be a creative professional to appreciate the screen.
The M6 Pro also provides three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot. The Air has two Thunderbolt 4 ports, so connecting memory cards, HDMI displays, or several accessories may require adapters or a dock.
For an OLED touchscreen, choose a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Touchscreen availability is a separate consideration from how much processing power you need.
Portability, battery life, and price
The Air is thinner and lighter, making it the stronger choice if you carry your laptop regularly. The 15-inch Air is also worth considering if you want a larger screen without the weight and expense of a 16-inch Pro.
The M6 MacBook Pro has a higher advertised battery-life rating, although actual endurance depends on your workload. Both models are suitable for working away from a power socket.
The Air costs less, but compare configurations with matching memory and storage before deciding. The M6 Pro starts with more storage, which narrows the price difference if you would otherwise upgrade the Air.
Our buying advice: Air or Pro?
Buy the MacBook Air for everyday work, studying, travel, and light creative projects. It offers the best balance of performance, portability, and price for most buyers.
Buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you want its HDR display, additional ports, longer advertised battery life, or better sustained performance.
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro for demanding professional workloads that justify more processing power, graphics performance, or memory. Consider the PROLED XDR version if you also want OLED and touch.

How long will a MacBook last?
The typical lifespan of a MacBook is generally between five and eight years, though this depends heavily on a combination of hardware durability and ongoing software support . While the physical components are built to last, Apple eventually classifies older models as “vintage” or “obsolete,” which limits your ability to get official repairs and parts. title: Apple’s new glowing logo on the MacBook Pro has a hidden on-off switch
content:
Macworld





With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. And it’s got a new trick: Turn up the display brightness, and the logo gets brighter, too. Turn down the display brightness, and the logo dims.
However, since the brightness controls on the display and logo are linked, the only way to turn the brightness on the logo all the way down is to also turn off the display. And sadly, Apple did not include a system setting control for the logo, so you can’t turn it off by simply flicking a switch.
But you can turn it off through Terminal, Apple’s command line interface for the Mac. In fact, Apple has a support document with the details.
Turn off the glowing Apple logo
You must be logged into the Mac with an account that has Administrator rights.
Launch Terminal. It is in Applications>Utilities. You can also press Command + Space to bring up Spotlight Search, type “Terminal,” and press Return after “Terminal — Open” appears in the search box.
Copy the following and paste it into Terminal sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0  then press Return
Terminal will ask for your password, which must be a user with Administrator rights. (When typing the password, Terminal will not show the characters.) Press Return and the logo should turn off.
Quit Terminal.
Turn on the glowing Apple logo
Follow the same steps as above, but enter this Terminal command: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode 
The glowing Apple logo is on by default, so if you reinstall macOS after turning it off, it will turn back on.
Or use a new app
Fortunately, now, there’s an app for that. Juan Buis created Backglow, a utility that can be used to customize the glowing Apple logo. In addition to turning it off and on, the free version of Backglow provides settings for two different pulse modes and it can remove the brightness limit. If you pay $9 for Backglow Pro, it activates the ability to set the glow pulse to music, and use Claude Code for your own personal pulse modes.

				
					

				
			Backglow can reside in the menu bar for quick access.

title: Some HomePod Mini 2 Buyers Returning Units Over Mac Speaker Issues
content:
One of the features of Apple's new HomePod mini 2 speakers is being able to use them as your Mac's default speakers, but it seems to be failing to work as advertised for a number of users, with some owners already returning them, based on the latest MacRumors forum reports.

OG HomePod minis in a stereo pair on a Mac (don't try this at home)

The new HomePod mini 2 can be used as a default speaker on all Mac models with Wi-Fi 6E or later, according to Apple. A single HomePod can be used alone, or a pair can be twinned for stereo sound. The same setup never reliably worked with the first-generation HomePod mini, with latency and dropout issues common.

HomePod‌ Software 27.2, and it's meant to work over "a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection," or a wireless point-to-point link that's designed to survive restarts and sleep. (That's different to ordinary AirPlay, which the previous-generation HomePod uses.) For the HomePod mini 2, the feature requires macOS 27.2. It's also supposed to work with the second-generation HomePod using the same software and the aforementioned Wi-Fi 6E requirement.

So far, new HomePod mini 2 owners are reporting two separate problems. For some, the option to enable the persistent connection never appears at all – even on hardware that meets Apple's stated requirements. For others, the connection works at first, but the Mac then falls back to its built-in or monitor speakers after sleep, a restart, or sometimes even after a single notification sound.

ran into the first problem in her review for The Verge. On a Mac mini M4 – meeting Apple's Wi-Fi 6E requirement – the persistent-output option never showed up, and the speakers behaved like ordinary AirPlay devices, along with audio artifacts, dropouts, and output switching after a restart or whenever Siri was activated on a HomePod. Tuohy said that the feature "feels unfinished," and Apple had not responded to her request for comment at the time of writing.

MacRumors forum reports. DanJoeWhitaker said they bought a stereo pair solely to use as Mac speakers, but found that the "Play sound effects through" option reverted to their Studio Display speakers within a minute, and that a single notification sound could make their Mac "forget" the HomePods entirely. 

Nismo73, tested a pair on a Mac Studio and was greeted by an error message and sound through the machine's internal speaker after the first wake from sleep. Five owners on the forums describe similar failures, and at least two forum members say they're returning the speakers. DanJoeWhitaker said they were told at an Apple Store that they weren't the first to have the problem – Apple Support's senior team reportedly offered no fix, suggesting the issue was "maybe just an early teething bug."

Redditor with an M3 Max MacBook Pro on a UniFi network. Their Mac's logs showed the point-to-point connection failing while the HomePods were on a 6GHz network, with audio falling back to standard AirPlay at around half a second of latency. Moving the speakers to a 5GHz-only network apparently restored the low-latency persistent mode in that setup. But whether the other failures correlate with 6GHz networks or specific router configurations remains unclear.

Photographers and designers14-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, non-touch)Excellent XDR display combined with CPU and GPU performance for creative applications.
Video editor (laptop)14-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro or M5 Max)Powerful media engines and sustained performance while remaining reasonably portable.
Video editor (desktop)Mac Studio (M5 Max)Powerful GPU and media capabilities make it ideal for demanding 4K/8K production workflows.
Creative professionals (desktop)Mac Studio (M5 Max)Workstation-class CPU and GPU performance for video, audio, photography, development and 3D work
Music productionMac Studio (M5 Max)Quiet operation, sustained CPU performance, lots of memory and extensive connectivity.
3D rendering Mac Studio (M5 Max or M5 Ultra)The most GPU performance and memory capacity.
Large AI modelsMac Studio (M5 Ultra)Up to 512GB of unified memory plus Apple’s highest-end CPU and GPU options.

 




 FAQ 


1.
What’s best, MacBook Air or MacBook Pro?
We explore this question in detail in our MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro comparison. The MacBook Air is the best choice for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work, studying and many creative tasks. The MacBook Pro is worth considering if you need sustained performance for demanding workloads, more ports or a more advanced display.
The entry-level MacBook Air costs $1,299/£1,299, although you can often spend less by shopping around – we regularly round up the best MacBook Air deals. If you want more screen space without paying for professional-level performance, the 15-inch MacBook Air is considerably cheaper than a 14-inch MacBook Pro.
Within the MacBook Pro range, the standard 14-inch M6 model provides a middle ground between the Air and the more expensive M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations. Its fan helps maintain performance during longer processing tasks, while its Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI port and SDXC card slot add flexibility.
The M5 Pro and M5 Max models suit more demanding professional workloads, offering more CPU and GPU cores, higher memory capacities and Thunderbolt 5. M5 Pro is a strong option for software development, photography and video editing. Consider M5 Max if your work benefits from its additional graphics power, media engines or higher memory ceiling; spending more won’t necessarily make everyday tasks noticeably faster.
You can also choose a MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR touchscreen. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, these models add an OLED display, touch controls alongside the keyboard and trackpad, Dynamic Island, and a thinner, lighter design. Starting at $2,899/£2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399/£3,399 for the 16-inch, they cost $400/£400 more than equivalent non-touch M5 Pro models. They use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip families, so the main reasons to pay extra are the display, portability and touch input.
Choosing between a 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro comes down to workspace, portability, battery life and price. The larger model gives you more room for editing timelines, coding and multitasking, while the 14-inch is easier to carry. Both sizes offer powerful Pro and Max configurations. For external monitors, current M5 Pro models support up to three displays and M5 Max models support up to four, depending on resolution and refresh rate.
For a tighter budget, the MacBook Neo lowers the starting price of a Mac laptop to $699/£699. It’s worth comparing its compromises with a discounted previous-generation MacBook Air before deciding.





2.
Should I upgrade from my Intel Mac?
Yes. It’s time! We are now more than six years into Apple’s transition from Intel processors to its own silicon that includes CPU, GPU, and unified memory. The transition began with the introduction of the M1 in November 2020. Since June 2023 every Mac Apple sells uses Apple’s own chips rather than Intel processors.
If you’ve yet to upgrade your Intel Mac to one powered by Apple’s silicon what are you waiting for? If you are concerned that a must-have app doesn’t run on an M-series Mac, consider finding a new app because the performance gains are tremendous.
Another good reason to replace an Intel Mac is that Apple’s support for these models is winding down. macOS Golden Gate, released in September 2026, is the first major version of macOS to support no Intel Macs. Intel Macs compatible with older versions of macOS may continue receiving security updates for a limited period, but they are now outside Apple’s current feature-release cycle. Apple does not guarantee how long those updates will continue, and machines limited to macOS Sequoia are likely to lose support sooner than those capable of running macOS Tahoe. Read: How long does Apple support Macs.





3.
Where can I get the best price for a new Mac?
Apple rarely offers direct price cuts on new hardware, but resellers frequently do. Getting the best price on a new Mac requires knowing where to look and when to buy: 
Top U.S. Retailers:
Amazon: Often has the lowest prices, especially during events like Prime Day. For example, during the July 2026 Prime Day event, a 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro was available for $1,749, a $450 discount. Even outside of events, Amazon frequently undercuts Apple’s MSRP.
Best Buy: A reliable source for discounts and trade-in offers. In late 2025, Best Buy offered a massive $1,150 off an M2 Ultra Mac Studio.
B&H Photo: A well-regarded authorized reseller that often has competitive pricing on Macs.
Walmart: Known for exclusive deals on older models, like the M1 MacBook Air, which has been sold brand-new for just $599.
Top U.K. Retailers:
Amazon UK: Similar to the U.S., Amazon UK is a primary source for discounts.
KRCS: An Apple Premium Reseller that frequently offers good deals.
John Lewis & Currys: Reliable high-street retailers that often have competitive prices and good customer service.
If you’re looking for a great offer, visit our Best Apple Deals page which is regularly updated.





4.
What specs do I really need for my Mac?
Chip: The specs you need depend on what you plan to do with your Mac. For web browsing, email, office apps and light photo editing, a standard M-series chip is more than sufficient. The M6 is available in the Mac mini, iMac and standard 14-inch MacBook Pro, while the MacBook Air uses M5. The budget MacBook Neo uses an A18 Pro chip. A newer generation number doesn’t automatically make a chip better for every workload: compare its CPU, GPU, memory and capabilities with what your apps actually need. 
If you regularly work with complex spreadsheets, large Photoshop files, audio projects, video editing or more demanding games, look at a Pro chip. The M5 Pro Mac mini, for example, offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU and up to 64GB unified memory.
A Max chip is worth considering for demanding graphics, complex 3D work, high-resolution video production or projects that need more memory than a Pro configuration supports. Many developers, photographers and video editors will be well served by a Pro chip. The M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and up to 128GB unified memory, depending on configuration. 
The M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 512GB unified memory, is aimed at the most extreme workloads, including VFX, scientific computing and running very large AI models locally.
GPU: One of the biggest differences between Apple’s chips is GPU performance. Standard M-series chips are easily sufficient for everyday graphics, casual gaming and light creative work. Pro chips add considerably more GPU power for video editing, graphics work, 3D applications and gaming. Max chips are designed for professional graphics, high-resolution video and demanding 3D workflows, while Ultra provides Apple’s highest GPU performance. The M5 Max offers up to 40 GPU cores, while the M5 Ultra doubles that to 80 GPU cores. Both also have Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to speed up AI workloads.
RAM: Apple calls RAM Unified Memory. The MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB, which is probably the biggest drawback of that machine. Most Macs start with at least 16GB, which is plenty for everyday use, although we recommend choosing more if your budget allows because the memory cannot be upgraded later. 24GB or 32GB is a good choice for heavier multitasking, photo editing, podcasting, moderate video production and gaming. Developers and professional creative users may benefit from 48GB, 64GB or more. The new M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 64GB, M5 Max Mac Studio with up to 128GB, and M5 Ultra Mac Studio with an enormous 512GB.
Storage: Even with iCloud and external drives available, it can seem like you can never have enough storage inside your Mac. 256GB may be sufficient for basic web and office use, but it can fill up quickly. We recommend 512GB for most people who want to keep a Mac for several years, particularly if you store photos, games or media locally. For regular video or audio production, 1TB or more is preferable. Professional users may need several terabytes. The M5 Pro Mac mini offers up to 8TB, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio and touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro offer up to 16TB. Maximum capacity varies by model and chip, so check the configuration you’re considering. Choose enough internal storage when ordering rather than relying on a later internal upgrade. An external SSD can add capacity for media libraries, project files and archives, often at a lower cost than Apple’s internal storage upgrades.
Display: Consider screen quality and workspace alongside processing power. The MacBook Air’s display is suitable for everyday work and many creative tasks, while MacBook Pro models add XDR brightness and ProMotion refresh rates. The PROLED XDR models also offer OLED, Adobe RGB support and touchscreen input in a lighter design. Choose them if those features will benefit how you work; they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip families as the non-touch versions.
For more information to help you decide which Mac to buy see our Mac processor comparison where we compare Apple silicon and Intel. We also offer advice about how much storage, RAM, and cores in How much MacBook RAM, SSD, GPU, and CPU do you really need.





5.
When were the Macs last updated?
In March 2026, Apple introduced the M5 MacBook Air, the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max, and the new MacBook Neo. All went on sale on March 11.
On August 25, 2026, Apple announced the Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro, and the Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra. Both ranges went on sale on September 22.
On October 27, 2026, Apple announced the M6 iMac and standard 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. The following day, it introduced the 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR displays and M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. In-store availability for these October models begins November 6.
Apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026. The Mac Studio is now its highest-end desktop Mac.





Why you can trust Macworld’s advice
Macworld has been covering everything Apple related since our first issue which arrived alongside the original Mac in 1984. Nobody knows Apple better, except probably Apple, but the difference is that we are completely impartial. We are made up of a team of experts with decades of experiences with Macs and other Apple products, and between us we have reviewed every Apple product meaning we are uniquely positioned to provide buying advice.
Price increases June 2026
In June 2026, Apple increased prices significantly across several product lines including Macs, iPads, the Apple TV 4K, and HomePod models, citing an unprecedented rise in component costs. 
The company stated it had “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly” and that it had shielded customers from these increases for as long as possible before finally raising prices. 
For Macs, prices increased from $100/£100 to $500/£500 depending on the model.
MacBook Neo is $100 more
MacBook Air is $200 more 
MacBook Pro is $300 to $500 more 
Mac mini was $200 more, but is now $300 more following the August update
Mac Studio is $500 more
Prices have been updated throughout this article.

content:

Our Verdict 
The SanDisk Extreme Pro delivers fast USB4 performance in a slim, lightweight design, with IP65 protection for life on the move. Strong write speeds suit demanding video and graphics work, although tested read speeds trail SanDisk’s claims. Its high price and lack of Thunderbolt 5 limit its appeal, but professionals prioritizing portability and durability will still find plenty to like.

What is it? A slim, rugged portable USB4 SSD with fast performance for storing and working with large files. 
Who’s it for? Professionals working with large video and graphics files who need fast, durable storage that’s easy to carry.
Who’s it not for? Budget-conscious buyers or professionals seeking the faster performance available from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD.
SanDisk has updated its entire range of portable solid-state drives, including this third-generation update for the Extreme Pro, which, as the name suggests, is aimed at professional users who need high-end performance when working with large video and graphics files. 
Sadly, like most forms of memory and storage, the Extreme Pro has rocketed in price since our review of the previous version, now starting at $549.99/£489.99 for a model with 2TB storage, or a whopping $1,099.99/£980.99 with 4TB. There’s also an 8TB model planned for next year, although SanDisk hasn’t given any indication of pricing for that model. 
You should also be aware that older versions of the drive are still widely available online, so make sure you select the correct model before buying. Alternatively, you could save some money by buying an older version of the drive – although, of course, it won’t be quite as fast as the latest model.
Design
The Extreme Pro is still an attractive option for professional users looking for a USB4 SSD to use with a Mac, though, with a more compact design than its predecessor, measuring just 110mm long, 58mm wide and 10mm thick, and weighing a mere 65.2g. It’s easy to slip it into a bag or jacket pocket if you’re travelling with your laptop, and there’s a clip for a lanyard (not included) on one corner of the drive to help keep it safe. It boasts a sturdy IP65 rating for weather-resistance, and Sandisk also states that it can survive being dropped from a height of three metres.
Performance
Performance is good too, with Sandisk quoting read and write speeds of 4GB/s and 3.8GB/s, respectively. The drive did fall a little short on read performance in our tests, using the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test, hitting around 3.5GB/s, but it outperformed on write performance, consistently reaching 4.2GB/s. 
The Extreme Pro will certainly be fast enough for pro users working with large video files, although it’s a shame that such an expensive drive is only using a USB4 interface, with no support for the even faster Thunderbolt 5 that is now available on several high-end Mac models.
Should you buy the SanDisk Extreme Pro?
The SanDisk Extreme Pro combines fast USB4 performance with a slim, lightweight design that’s easy to carry alongside your MacBook. Strong write speeds make it appealing for professionals working with large video and graphics files, while IP65 protection and claimed three-meter drop resistance add reassurance when traveling. 
However, read speeds fell short of SanDisk’s claims in our tests, and the lack of Thunderbolt 5 feels disappointing at this price. Starting at $549.99/£489.99 for 2TB, it’s a costly investment. It’s worth considering if portability, durability, and speed are priorities, but the steep price makes it harder to recommend without some reservations.

title: Siri Is Getting a Better Memory
content:
Apple is building a personal memory system that could help Siri retain information about users' lives, based on new code findings shared by code explorer pdfu.


In Apple's iOS 27.3 beta release, the system includes a "memory graph" that's designed to organize information about relationships, places, routines, health, workouts, and what motivates users or holds them back, according to the findings. It also identifies "memory atoms" for facts, opinions, intentions, and events, including details about the people, places, times, and topics involved.

According to pdfu, the graph uses two kinds of processes to gather info. One turns structured data into insights – like reading the name fields in a user's own contact card. The other uses an on-device AI model or Private Cloud Compute to extract insights by querying sources including Siri conversations, messages, photos, and health data.

Apparently, only one of these AI-driven processes is present so far: pdfu believes it's designed to identify motivations, barriers, and resources using a set of 60 built-in questions, including questions about routines that might interfere with adequate sleep.

follow-up explanation, the code sleuth also distinguished the graph from a separate store for explicit memories. The latter store has space for records in Apple's search system, but nothing writes the records yet.
