title: iOS 27: What’s new, what’s in the latest beta and what’s coming next
content:
Macworld





Apple unveiled iOS 27 at WWDC on June 8, 2026, with the public release following on September 14. The latest update, iOS 27.2.1 arrived on November 9, with security fixes. It follows the October 26 release of iOS 27.2, which introduced further Siri AI improvements and new app features. 
iOS 27 mainly focuses on three key areas: Siri AI, a rebuilt assistant with its own dedicated app; new child safety and parental controls; and system improvements designed to make everyday tasks faster and easier.
iOS 27 supports the iPhone 11 and later, plus the iPhone SE (2nd generation) and later, although some Apple Intelligence and Siri features require newer hardware.
This guide covers iOS 27’s biggest new features, compatible iPhones, the latest beta developments and the promised features still to come in future updates.


What’s New in iOS 27 at a Glance
Siri AI: Apple’s new Siri AI combines personal context, onscreen awareness and web knowledge to deliver more natural conversations, richer answers, app actions and cross-device chat history.
Apple Intelligence across apps: Apple Intelligence expands across Safari, Photos, Messages, Mail, Calendar, Home and Shortcuts, adding smarter suggestions, automation, image generation and context-aware assistance.
Smarter Photos editing: Photos gains Spatial Reframing, Extend and an upgraded Clean Up tool, allowing users to improve composition, expand images and remove distractions more naturally.
Child safety and parental controls: New parental controls include Ask to Browse, Time Allowances, app schedules and enhanced Communication Safety tools. Activating the redesigned experience through Family Sharing requires every eligible family device to be running version 27 or later.
System Improvements: Apple has made many system operations faster and more efficient, which will be especially noticeable on older phones. Battery life may be longer, and there are dozens of small quality-of-life improvements throughout the system and its apps.
iPhone Handoff: iPhone Handoff in iOS 27 lets two eSIM-equipped iPhones share one number, switching calls, messages and Find My location when unlocked. It requires matching Apple Accounts and carrier support. T-Mobile offers it; Verizon and EE plan support. Fees may apply. More information below.


						

							


iOS 27 latest version: What’s in iOS 27.2.1
Apple released iOS 27.2.1 on November 9, 2026. The update fixes security vulnerabilities affecting AirPlay, Bluetooth, Messages and other system components. These include flaws that could allow unauthorized access to iMessage group conversations and Bluetooth pairing without user interaction.
iOS 27 version history: Every update and release date
What did iOS 27.0.1 add? The first update was iOS 27.0.1, released on September 28. It fixed unexpected restarts following failed Face ID authentication, a 2x-camera color artifact affecting iPhone 18 Pro models, and an iOS 27 touchscreen freeze triggered by opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously. iOS 27.0.1 also has a preventive role in a cellular problem that Apple did not mention in its published release notes. Apple confirmed that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max models on AT&T can lose cellular service, preventing calls, texts and data access and potentially affecting 911 calls. Some owners reported their phones dropping into SOS mode despite previously showing a strong 5G signal.
What did iOS 27.1 add? Apple released iOS 27.1 on October 23, 2026, exclusively for the iPhone Duo; other iPhone models moved directly from iOS 27.0.1 to iOS 27.2.
What did iOS 27.2 add? Apple released iOS 27.2 on October 26, 2026. It improves Siri AI’s memory and personal context, expands language support, and adds Suggestions in Messages alongside other app improvements, bug fixes and security updates. Dual Capture arrives for Group FaceTime calls, while iPhone Duo gains Apple Pencil (USB-C) support and Edge Light to illuminate your face during video calls. Shared Albums in Photos gains editable captions and comments, helps avoid duplicate photos, and provides reminders to save photos and videos before temporary albums expire. Read our iOS 27.2 guide for more details.


						

							


iOS 27 beta – What’s coming next?
Latest developer beta: iOS 27.3 beta 1, released November 3, 2026.
Latest public beta: iOS 27.3 public beta 1, released November 5, 2026.
Apple has begun testing iOS 27.3. Changes reported in the first version of the beta include:
Redesigned Health app: The new design returns after appearing briefly during iOS 27.2 testing.
Apple Watch Audio Intelligence: Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available for testing with an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4.
More Siri AI languages: Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese are being tested.
Expanded Siri actions: Siri gains more capabilities within Apple’s apps, while developers can begin testing new integrations for third-party apps.
Apple Intelligence in China: Initial features include Writing Tools, Visual Intelligence, Clean Up and Genmoji. Siri AI remains unavailable.
iPhone Duo Reachability: Content can shift sideways to make the wider display easier to reach.
iCloud public-link checks: Apple says that starting with iOS 27.3, it will check photos, files and other iCloud content shared using “Anyone with the link” for harmful content. These items are accessible to Apple and aren’t end-to-end encrypted, even if Advanced Data Protection is enabled. The checks apply to items shared through this public-link option, rather than everything stored in iCloud. To restrict access to invited recipients, choose “People you choose” when sharing.


						

							


What features are still to come in iOS 27
At the time of the launch of iOS 27 not all of Apple’s promised features were available. Several were added in iOS 27.2, but there are still a couple that we’re waiting on.
Redesigned Health app: Having been removed in earlier beta testing, the new Health app design has returned in the iOS 27.3 beta.
Automatic password changes: The ability for the Passwords app to visit supported websites and automatically replace compromised passwords was removed shortly before release. 


						

							


What does Siri AI do in iOS 27

				
					

				
			
Apple




By far the biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI – an entirely new architecture for Siri. Apple says it is more personal, conversational, and capable than the current assistant, with support for natural follow-up questions, personal context, onscreen awareness and up-to-date information from the web.
Siri AI features
More natural conversations: Siri AI can understand open-ended questions, follow-up requests and more complex natural language, making interactions feel less like issuing simple voice commands.
Personal context: Siri can draw on information stored in Messages, Mail, Photos and Notes to find details and answer questions. For example, you could ask it to find information buried in an old email or message.
Onscreen awareness: Siri can understand what you’re viewing and act on it, such as saving an address from a message, adding an event to Calendar or answering questions about an article.
Camera intelligence: A new Siri Camera mode lets you show Siri something through the iPhone’s camera, then ask questions or perform actions based on what it sees.
More capable app actions: Siri can perform tasks within apps such as Messages, Music and Reminders. It can, for example, edit a recently sent message, add a song to a playlist or handle more complex Apple Music requests.
Better general knowledge and web answers: Siri can use information from the web to answer questions about recent events and tackle more specific or complicated queries than before.
Conversation history across devices: A dedicated Siri app lets users revisit previous conversations, pin important chats and continue conversations across Apple devices using iCloud syncing.
More natural Siri voices: Siri gains more expressive voices, with controls on compatible devices for adjusting speaking pace and expressiveness. Voice customization requires an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air or newer.
Improved dictation: Better speech recognition, automatic punctuation, capitalization and formatting allow users to dictate more naturally when converting speech into text.
AI-assisted message replies: Siri can compose contextual replies in Messages using the conversation, personal information and web searches. Shortcuts can also automate replies to selected contacts, although manual Siri-assisted replies allow users to check and edit the response before it is sent.
iOS 27.2 added several further Siri AI improvements:
Recall information from previous conversations.
Use Messages photo attachments, Calendar attendees and voicemails, with better results from Safari history and Reading List.
Control app access for Siri, Search and suggestions through Excluded Apps.
Select and copy individual portions of Siri’s responses.
iOS 27.3 expands Siri’s actions across Apple apps, including Calendar, Messages, Music and Reminders. You can ask Siri what it can do within an app.
Apple has also opened a developer preview that lets third-party apps connect their content and actions to Siri AI. This requires developers to build support into their apps. Apple says App Store submissions using these capabilities will open in spring, so installing iOS 27.3 alone will not enable the new integrations across existing apps.
If you haven’t got Siri AI yet find out how here: Why don’t I have Siri AI on my iPhone?
Read about what happened when we made Siri AI Answer all our Messages.
How good is Siri AI?
Siri AI represents a significant improvement over the old Siri, particularly when handling conversational questions, current information, and personal context. It also has a dedicated app where you can see and continue previous conversations, upload images or documents, and more.
Even in our early tests during the beta, Siri AI proved to be much more helpful and useful. 
It’s definitely one of the biggest reasons to upgrade to iOS 27, potentially changing Siri from a basic voice-command system into a more general way of interacting with the iPhone.
Apple’s approach to AI safety also appears more restrained than some rival chatbots, with Siri designed to avoid excessive flattery, pretending to be human, or responding inappropriately to potentially harmful requests.
Siri AI remains a beta feature. iOS 27.2 added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish alongside English. Siri AI remains unavailable on iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch in the EU and mainland China. The EU restriction does not apply to Siri AI on Mac so Siri AI can be used on the Mac in the EU.
Regional Siri AI availability
Siri AI will not initially be available on iPhone or iPad in the EU. It will also remain unavailable in China while Apple works through regulatory issues. 
The first release only supported the English language, and initially had only Expressive Voices for English (UK) and English (US). Support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish arrived with iOS 27.2. 
Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese support is being tested in the iOS 27.3 beta. Siri AI is still not available in mainland China.
Lack of Siri language support is separate to Apple Intelligence language support. 
Siri AI compatibility
Siri AI requires iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, and all iPhone 16 models and later, and the “new expressive voices” feature requires an iPhone 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max and currently supports US and UK English voices.
Siri AI age restriction: Siri AI is unavailable to children under 13.


						

							


Apple Intelligence across apps
As well as Siri AI, the enhanced Apple Intelligence will power new features in Apple’s core apps throughout iOS 27. Safari can organize tabs into topics, monitor webpages for changes and even build extensions from natural-language descriptions. Photos gains a new Spatial Reframing editing tools including an upgraded Clean Up feature. Messages, Mail, and Calendar can now understand context, suggest actions and create events from simple descriptions.
Usage limits: Some cloud-based Apple Intelligence features have daily limits. The limits cover Siri AI as well as other cloud-based Apple Intelligence features, including intelligent photo editing, Image Playground and cloud models in Shortcuts. Apple says expanded access will be available for a fee in future.


						

							


New features coming to apps in iOS 27
iOS 27 brings a mix of major Apple Intelligence upgrades and smaller quality-of-life improvements across Safari, Photos, Messages, AirPods, Passwords, Wallet, and other core iPhone apps. Apple is also making iOS more adaptable to different screen sizes and orientations, which are changes necessary for the iPhone Duo.
Safari
Safari can automatically group open tabs into topics, making related pages easier to find. A new Notify Me feature will monitor webpages and alert you to changes such as price drops or products coming back into stock.
There’s also a new Describe an Extension feature which lets users create custom Safari extensions simply by explaining what they want the extension to do.

				
					

				
			

Apple




Photos
Photos gains significantly more powerful AI editing tools.
Reframe can alter the composition and perspective of an existing photo, while Extend generates new image content beyond the original frame when straightening a horizon or changing the aspect ratio.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Clean Up has also been improved, with Fast and High Quality modes for removing unwanted objects or details. High Quality mode can produce considerably more natural results, although more ambitious edits can still introduce distortions or invented details.
Photos also adds new categories and the ability to save a frame from a video as a full-resolution photo. The resulting HEIF or JPG retains the video’s original resolution, date, and location metadata rather than simply creating a screenshot.
Camera
iOS 27 features a new more customizable camera interface that lets you pin the controls you use most often. For the iPhone 18 Pro, there are also “pro controls” like white balance, shutter speed, and manual focus along with Apple Reference Image, an authentication system designed to prove that a photo or video was genuinely captured on an iPhone and has not subsequently been manipulated.
The new Siri mode in the Camera app is a more convenient and logical way to access the Visual Intelligence features that used to require either a long-press of the camera button or a Control Center button.
Messages

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Messages gets several useful improvements.
You can decide what the microphone button beside the text field does. Under Settings > Apps > Messages > Show in Text Field, it can be set to Record Audio, Start Dictation, or None. Disabling it does not remove either feature: dictation remains available from the keyboard and audio messages remain in the + menu.
Voice-message playback controls are easier to access. 
iOS 27.2 adds Suggestions in Messages, which uses the context of your conversations to suggest actions in apps such as Calendar and Reminders. For example, when you discuss dinner plans, Messages can suggest creating a Calendar invitation.
Messages in iOS 27 will gain smarter suggested replies that can better reflect the user’s writing style. (This was removed from the iOS 27 beta and wasn’t available at the launch of iOS 27).
Drawing

				
					

				
			
Foundry




A new dedicated Drawing app replaces the old hidden handwriting interface. Accessible from the + menu, it uses the familiar pens, colours and drawing controls found in Notes and Markup, with finished drawings sent as images.
Mail
Mail gains more context-aware smart replies, including responses that can better match the user’s usual writing style.
Apple Intelligence can also surface information from Mail elsewhere in iOS. For example, the Phone app could retrieve a flight confirmation number from an email when you call an airline.
Phone
A new Call Context feature can surface information that may be useful when on a call. Apple says the information is selected according to who you are calling rather than by listening to the conversation. For example, calling an airline could cause iOS to surface the relevant flight confirmation from Mail.
Birthday reminders can also appear when calling contacts whose birthdays are stored on the iPhone.
iPhone Handoff
iPhone Handoff in iOS 27 lets you switch between two iPhones while keeping the same phone number. The number is active on only one iPhone at a time. When you unlock one of the two iPhones, your calls, voicemail, messages—including SMS and RCS—and your Find My location will be linked to that iPhone. 
The feature will work on any iPhone running iOS 27, as long as it has an eSIM. Both phones must use the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled and matching FaceTime/iMessage sign-ins. 
You will need a carrier and eligible plan that specifically support iPhone Handoff – an ordinary eSIM plan alone isn’t enough. In the U.S. T-Mobile offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month and Verizon has announced support for later in 2026. In the U.K. EE has announced that support for iPhone Handoff is coming soon for £5 a month. 
FaceTime
Dual Capture arrived in iOS 27.2, allowing Group FaceTime participants to share front- and rear-camera views simultaneously. 
iOS 27.2 also adds support for bringing a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner into a FaceTime call, providing additional communication support for participants.
Passwords

				
					

				
			
Passwords in iOS 27 will fix things for you.

Apple




The Passwords app continues to warn about weak, reused and compromised credentials, but iOS 27 will go a step further – eventually. Automatic password changes are coming to the Passwords app in a future software update. Apple has not confirmed a release date.
The forthcoming feature will, with your permission, visit supported websites, change vulnerable passwords and save the replacement credentials automatically. See: Apple got rid of my biggest password headache.
The usefulness of the feature will depend on how widely websites are supported and how well it handles obstacles such as two-factor authentication and unusual account-management interfaces. 
Apple removed this ability to detect compromised passwords and replace them from the beta shortly before the release of iOS 27. It’s expected to arrive with a later update.
Shortcuts
Shortcuts gains Describe a Shortcut, allowing users to create automations simply by explaining what they want to happen.
Apple Intelligence interprets the request and assembles the appropriate actions across supported apps, potentially making Shortcuts significantly easier to use for people unfamiliar with building automations manually.
Calendar
Calendar can create or modify events from natural-language instructions.
Apple says the app can recognize contacts, locations, dates and other event details as users type, reducing the amount of information that needs to be entered manually.
Siri can also create complete Calendar entries for information that is on your screen in that moment, or by taking a picture with the Siri mode in the Camera app.
Image Playground
Image Playground is considerably more powerful and realistic.
Apple says it can create photorealistic images and lets users modify generated pictures simply by describing the changes they want. Individual objects can also be selected, resized, or repositioned.
iOS 27.2 adds SynthID support to help identify images generated or modified using Photos and Image Playground.
Wallet
Wallet can create custom passes from QR codes.
Users can add their own fields and information to the pass, and passes automatically sync to Apple Watch.
Weather
Weather gets a clearer, more detailed forecast interface, with rearranged information tiles and new 10-day views showing precipitation probability/amount and wind speed throughout each day.
Home app
Apple Intelligence comes to the Home app for compatible HomeKit Secure Video cameras. It can group related camera notifications, describe recorded video and highlight clips that appear particularly noteworthy.
Maps
Apple Maps improves Flyover using higher-quality aerial imagery and Visual Intelligence models.
Apple says this produces sharper architectural detail and more realistic rendering of elements such as individual trees.
Podcasts
Video podcasts become easier to use, with improved controls for switching between watching a podcast and simply listening to it.
iOS 27.2 also reorganizes the Podcasts app’s Home tab into two separate sections: New Episodes, where you can find the latest releases from shows you follow, and Continue Playing, where you can resume episodes you’ve already started. This makes it easier to distinguish new listening from unfinished episodes.
Fitness
Workout summaries have been redesigned to make them easier to share.
Users can also hide completed Fitness+ workouts.
Games 
iOS 27.2 improves the Games app’s Friends tab with more information about suggested friends. Friends’ player pages also show the games they’ve played recently, making it easier to find something to play together.
Apple TV 
iOS 27.2 adds Simple Profiles to the Apple TV app, allowing members of your household to have their own profiles with recommendations tailored to their viewing preferences.


						

							


iOS 27 changes beyond the iPhone 
CarPlay
CarPlay gains an audio scrubber, giving drivers and passengers more direct control when moving through audio tracks and other content.
AirPods
iOS 27 introduces several new AirPods features.
A new Custom EQ lets users independently adjust bass, mids and treble using a simple three-band equalizer under Settings > AirPods > Audio and Routing > Equalizer > Custom.
Compatible AirPods also gain improved Precision Finding through Find My, making individual earbuds easier to locate.
Some features require both iOS 27 and compatible AirPods firmware.
Read How to tune your AirPods with a custom EQ in iOS 27.


						

							


Other changes in iOS 27
It’s not only individual apps that are seeing changes.
Home Screen and landscape mode
Apple is making iOS significantly more flexible when dealing with different screen orientations and sizes.
More Apple apps now work properly in landscape, including Health, Home, Music, Weather, and Watch. Dynamic Island and Live Activities can also adapt to landscape orientation. The Home Screen supports extra-large widgets.
These changes could simply improve iPhone usability, but they’re also well suited to Apple’s folding iPhone Duo.
iPhone Mirroring in macOS 27 has similarly become freely resizable, with Apple apps dynamically rearranging their interfaces as the window changes shape.
Liquid Glass refinements

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple says Liquid Glass has been refined for better readability, more uniform refraction and improved contrast. A new slider lets users adjust the look from ultraclear to fully tinted, while updated icons, toolbars, sidebars and window shapes add polish.
Ringtones, alarms and alert volume
iOS 27 finally separates several sound-volume controls.
Instead of one combined Ringtone and Alerts slider, users can independently adjust:
Ringtones
Alarms and timers
Alerts and system sounds
The change is optional. Under Settings > Sounds & Haptics, turning off Match Ringtone Volume reveals separate controls.
Media and call volume continue to work independently as before.
Keyboard
iOS 27 introduces a new quick-paste control above the keyboard.
It lets you paste recently copied text, images or screenshots without having to long-press inside a text field, making everyday copy-and-paste considerably faster.
Apple has also made the Liquid Glass keyboard design more consistent across apps.
Privacy and Find My
iOS 27 introduces the ability to temporarily pause Find My location sharing without notifying the person with whom the location is normally shared.
Recovery and troubleshooting
Apple is also expanding the iPhone’s recovery interface, giving users more options for diagnosing problems and recovering an iPhone without immediately connecting it to another device.


						

							


System changes and how iOS 27 makes your iPhone faster
Alongside the headline AI features, Apple says iOS 27 includes a wide range of under-the-hood improvements designed to make iPhones faster, smoother and more efficient.
Apps can launch up to 30% faster, newly taken photos can appear in the Photos library up to 70% faster, and AirDrop transfers can be up to 80% quicker. External drive transfers should also improve, while updates to network performance and the system-wide search index are designed to make connectivity and finding information faster.
The company has also reworked core technologies including CPU scheduling, display performance and processing efficiency. These changes should benefit older iPhones in particular, with Apple promising smoother performance and more efficient battery use on devices as old as the iPhone 11 and second-generation iPhone SE.
Our testing of the iOS 27 beta supports those claims. On an iPhone 11 Pro Max, Camera launch time fell from 0.98 seconds in iOS 26 to 0.65 seconds in iOS 27, while Maps improved from 3.01 seconds to 1.36 seconds.
Everyday use also feels smoother, with more fluid animations, unlocking, Control Center and app transitions. The phone ran cooler during testing too, which could point to improved system efficiency and potentially better battery performance.
More broadly, iOS 27 appears focused on refinement rather than simply adding new features. Apple says it has addressed dozens of common user frustrations, while changes such as more adjustable Liquid Glass effects are intended to improve readability and general usability.
That focus should make iOS 27 particularly worthwhile for owners of older iPhones, even on models that do not support Siri AI. Those devices still gain performance improvements alongside features such as clipboard tools for the keyboard, independent alarm and timer volume controls, custom Wallet passes, Photos changes, larger widgets, and Liquid Glass refinements.


						

							


Child safety and parental controls

				
					

				
			
Apple




There are lots of improvements to parental controls, including new time allowances for entertainment, games, and social media, and new schedule tools for different times of day or days of the week.
This includes new features like an expansion of the existing “ask to buy” feature for apps to websites. Before a child can view a new website, they’ll have to ask for permission.
Ask to Browse: Will expand the current Ask to Buy feature to the web. Children will need to request permission before visiting new websites, and parents can review requests in Messages before approving.
Communication Safety: Communication Safety continues to help protect children from viewing or sharing nudity in Messages, FaceTime and other apps. Apple says it will also intervene before children see gore or violent content in shared images and videos.
Time Allowances and schedules: Parents can set Time Allowances across categories such as Entertainment, Games and Social Media. Recommendations are based on a child’s age combined with guidance from clinical and child development experts. Schedules let parents choose which apps are available at different times or on different days.
Redesigned Screen Time: Screen Time gets a redesigned interface with an at-a-glance view of average device usage and most-used apps. Apple says parents can quickly limit or extend access in the moment.
Child accounts and family safety: Apple says child accounts remain central to age-appropriate protections. Parents can manage app access, web access, communication permissions and Screen Time settings. 
Problems with Parental Control setup
Updating the parent’s iPhone is not enough to activate the redesigned Screen Time experience. Apple says every eligible iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro in the Family Sharing group must be running the appropriate version 27 software.
Devices that cannot run version 27 are listed as Legacy Devices and can continue using the older Screen Time and Family Sharing system. Apple says these incompatible devices should not prevent supported devices from adopting the new controls.
To find out which devices need to be updated go to Settings > Family > View Family Devices. Once eligible devices are running iOS 27, go to Settings > Family > Get Started to transfer the family’s existing parental controls or set up new ones.
Some families have encountered delays, outdated device listings and eligible hardware incorrectly appearing not to have been updated. Apple has acknowledged the rollout problems and says it is working to resolve them. If an eligible device is no longer owned or accessible, Apple recommends removing it from the Apple Account device list.


						

							


Accessibility changes in iOS 27
Accessibility features are smarter and more intuitive in iOS 27:
VoiceOver gives richer image descriptions and better understanding of onscreen content.
Live Recognition lets users press the Action button to ask questions about their surroundings and receive detailed responses.
Voice Control is more intuitive, allowing users to describe onscreen buttons and controls rather than remembering exact coordinate labels or numbers.
Accessibility Reader is able to handle more complex source material and provide summaries and translation.


						

							


iOS 27 compatibility 

				
					

				
			iPhone 11 is supported by iOS 27.
Roman Loyola/IDG




According to Apple, iOS 27 supports iPhones back to the iPhone 11 and second-generation iPhone SE, although some Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features require newer hardware.
Support for iOS 27 does not mean every device gets every feature. Apple Intelligence and Siri AI require an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 or later, while the most advanced on-device AI models require an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or iPhone 18 Pro. On iPad, Apple Intelligence requires an M1-class model or the A17 Pro iPad mini, while the newest on-device models require an M4 iPad with at least 12GB of RAM.
There had been speculation that the iPhone 11 series and iPhone SE 2 would miss out on iOS 27 after leaker Instant Digital claimed on Weibo that the 2019 iPhone 11, 11 Pro and 11 Pro Max, along with the 2020 iPhone SE 2, would no longer be supported. That prediction proved incorrect, giving those models at least one more year of software support.
However, the iPhone 11 generation is nearing the end of its support life. As we explain in our guide to how long Apple supports iPhones, the iPhone 11 Pro and 11 Pro Max have already been added to Apple’s Vintage iPhone list.
The iOS 27 compatibility list is:
iPhone 18 Pro
iPhone 18 Pro Max
iPhone Duo
iPhone 17e (launched in 2026) 
iPhone 17, 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max (launched in 2025)
iPhone Air (launched in 2025)
iPhone 16e (launched in 2025)
iPhone 16 / 16 Plus and iPhone 16 Pro / 16 Pro Max (launched in 2024)
iPhone 15 / 15 Plus and iPhone 15 Pro / 15 Pro Max (launched in 2023)
iPhone 14 / 14 Plus / 14 Pro / 14 Pro Max (launched in 2022)
iPhone SE 3 (launched in 2022)
iPhone 13 / 13 mini / 13 Pro / 13 Pro Max (launched in 2021)
iPhone 12 / 12 mini / 12 Pro / 12 Pro Max (launched in 2020)
iPhone SE 2 (launched in 2020)
iPhone 11 / 11 Pro / 11 Pro Max (launched in 2019)
The main dividing line for Apple Intelligence remains the iPhone 15 Pro generation: the standard iPhone 15 and all older models can run iOS 27, but they do not support Apple Intelligence.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
When was iOS 27 released?
iOS 27 was released on September 14, 2026.





2.
Which iPhones get iOS 27?
The iPhone 11 and iPhone SE 2 and newer get iOS 27. However, Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features require iPhone 15 Pro or newer, and the new more expressive Siri voices feature requires iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, or newer.





3.
Which iPhones will get Siri AI and Apple Intelligence in iOS 27?
The only iPhones that can run Siri AI are the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max and any newer generation. If you have a standard iPhone 15 then you won’t get Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.

title: iPhone 18e Could Feature Bigger Display and Battery
content:
Apple's standard iPhone 18 and the lower-cost iPhone 18e will both feature 6.3-inch displays and use the same battery, according to the leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital."


In a new post on Weibo, the leaker shared an annotated, side-by-side diagram of the phones' purported internals, labeled "Taycan" for the ‌iPhone 18‌ and "Nevera" for the iPhone 18e. Fixed Focus Digital said the diagram was already circulating online and broadly matched what their sources had told them. They pointed to the battery as an example of the interchangeable parts they had previously described.

The diagram's annotations list a 4,430 mAh battery for both models. That would be an increase of about 21% from 3,671 mAh for the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and about 11% from 4,005 mAh for the iPhone 18e. The notes attribute the extra room in the standard model to changes to the bottom speaker and haptic engine. The diagram also shows two rear cameras on the standard ‌iPhone 18‌, including an Ultra Wide camera, and a single rear camera on the iPhone 18e, just like previous models.

iPhone 17e. Fellow Weibo leaker "Digital Chat Station" previously claimed the iPhone 18e would retain a 6.12-inch OLED display at 60Hz, along with a single 48-megapixel rear camera and a potential upgrade to the front-facing camera. The same source expects the standard iPhone 18 to retain its 6.3-inch display with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz, along with a larger battery.

earlier post, Fixed Focus Digital said a new chip was the only iPhone 18e upgrade they could confirm at the time and suggested the two models would share some manufacturing processes.

3nm A19 in the ‌iPhone 17e‌. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo has said Apple's lower-end spring 2027 iPhones will pair the A20 chip with 9GB of RAM, up from 8GB. Both models are also rumored to get Apple's C2 modem, which would replace the Snapdragon X80 in the iPhone 17 and the C1X in the ‌iPhone 17e‌.

expected to launch in spring 2027 alongside the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and second-generation iPhone Air. The ‌iPhone 17e‌ launched at $599 with 256GB of storage, and it is unclear if it will get a price increase like other iPhone models.

title: Apple's Siri Boss May Leave - Here's Who Could Take Over
content:
Mike Rockwell "continues to seriously consider stepping down" as Apple's vice president of Siri engineering and could leave the company altogether next year, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Gurman described the potential move as a major blow to Apple.


If Rockwell departs or moves to another role, responsibility for Siri would likely fall to one of two people. Amar Subramanya is a Google veteran hired last year to shore up Apple's AI efforts, and Sebastien Marineau, a deputy to software chief Craig Federighi, leads the teams integrating AI into iOS. Marineau is said to be seen by some inside Apple as a possible eventual successor to Federighi himself, and as someone "more all-in on the AI revolution."

Reports of him weighing an exit from Apple first surfaced in April.

Tags: Mark Gurman, Siri, Siri AI

title: Apple Stores ordered to stop signing up unwitting customers to services
content:
Staff at Apple Stores have been pressured into signing up customers to services such as Apple TV, but the practice has reportedly been stopped after it was uncovered.


No specific Apple Stores have been identified over this subscription practice, but reportedly all stores have been directed to stop. This is Tysons Corner Apple Store in 2023.
Apple has previously cracked down on other firms pushing subscriptions on unwitting users, but now it has been doing something similar. Whether Apple expressly sanctioned it or just created the pressure on its employees, staff at Apple Stores have reportedly been signing up users to free trials without telling them.
The practice was uncovered by Louis Rossmann, previously best known as a critic of Apple's repair policies. In the latest of a series of YouTube videos, he has explained how the practice worked.

title: 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: Simply irresistible
content:

Touch input

Our Verdict 
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display raises the bar of Apple excellence. It’s a landmark addition to the Mac lineup, and it’s a reminder of what makes users devoted to the Mac. It’s a good time to be a Mac user.

With its newest MacBook, Apple takes the idea of a Pro laptop to another level. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the most expensive model in the lineup. It’s made to appeal to the most demanding professionals, especially those who take content creation seriously and are willing to pay a premium.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t for everyone, but even if you don’t fit into its intended audience, you will want this laptop. All it takes is one look. It is glorious, it is profound, and it is effing awesome–pardon my thinly-veiled language, but that’s just how I feel about this laptop. This, dear reader, is Apple’s finest MacBook to date and probably the best laptop ever made.
Our model’s specifications
This review looks at a model that’s been customized from Apple’s standard offerings. It has some hefty add-ons that increase the price significantly. Here are the specifications of the laptop in this review:
CPU: M5 Max with an 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores); 16-core Neural Engine
GPU: 40 cores
Memory: 128GB unified memory
Storage: 2TB SSD
Display: 16.3-inch tandem OLED; 3472-by-2266 native resolution at 254 pixels per inch; 1000 nits sustained XDR brightness, 2000 nits peak (HDR content only); 1000 nits SDR brightness, 2000 nits peak (outdoor); 1 billion colors; P3 + Adobe RGB wide color gamut; True Tone; standard glass
Ports: 3 Thunderbolt 5/USB-C; MagSafe 3; SDXC Card slot; HDMI; 3.5mm audio
Networking: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be); Bluetooth 6; Thread
Input devices: Touchscreen; Magic Keyboard with Touch ID; Magic Trackpad
Weight: 4.1 pounds (1.84 kg)
Dimensions: 0.63 x 14.0 x 9.62 inches (1.60 x 35.55 x 24.42 cm)
Price (as tested): $7,399/£7,399

				
					

				
			
The touchscreen MacBook Pro’s OLED display offers new highs in brightness and great color fidelity

Roman Loyola/Foundry




PROLED MacBook Pro: Display
As the name implies, the tandem OLED display is the key feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. This is the main reason to spend the extra $400 over the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED backlit display.
When I unpacked the laptop, opened it for the first time, and the display lit up, I instantly knew I was in for a special experience. The brightness of the tandem OLED makes an immediate impression. With the right wallpaper, such as the macOS Golden Gate default photo, the brightness gives the image an aura that feels magical.
It’s an admirable feat to outdo the mini-LED backlit displays that Apple replaced, because they’re excellent displays in their own right. The tandem OLED is more than up to the task. Color saturation and evenness are more pleasing, and the contrast and blacks are deeper. At the Macworld office, my desk is set up with a first-generation Apple Studio Display and a Dell UltraSharp 32 4K QD-OLED Monitor U3226Q, which is made for production work. Yet I prefer looking at the PROLED XDR Display. You will want to work on photos, video, and graphics on this MacBook Pro.
If that work takes you outside, well, don’t worry. I’m currently writing this display section of the review in my backyard, because it’s a perfect San Francisco day, a bright and sunny 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20°C). It’s early afternoon, and the sun is bearing down directly on the display and me. Yet the screen shines through like a champ. Glare and reflections? No problem, thanks to the OLED’s brightness working with the antireflective coating on the glass. Don’t hesitate to go outside or take this MacBook Pro on location. I’d actually stay outside longer if it wasn’t for the fact that the sun is starting to cook me, which makes me a little concerned about the laptop heating up, too.

				
					

				
			
MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display with standard glass (left) is much more visbile in direct sunlight than the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED backlit Nano-texture glass display (right).

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Since this is the first time OLED is on the Mac, you might be concerned about burn-in–if you’re going to spend the extra $400, it better last. Only time will tell with the new MacBook Pro, but Apple updated the display engine for OLED, and it monitors the OLED’s condition to maintain optimal performance and minimize the burn-in risk. Apple uses OLED displays in its iPhones, and it introduced a tandem OLED in the iPad Pro in 2024. We haven’t heard of widespread burn-in problems with those devices.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Touch UI
There’s been a lot of anticipation about this being Apple’s first touchscreen Mac. Touchscreen Windows laptops have long been available, and Apple has repeatedly said that touchscreen input on the Mac wasn’t going to happen. Times change. Generations of people have grown up with touch interfaces, and the lack of touch on the Mac is something that prevented some from switching from Windows. There’s a demand for touch.

				
					

				
			Touch on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is responsive, and macOS’s main elements have been adjusted to accommodate fingers.
Roman Loyola/Foundry




I wrote a separate article that details the Touch experience, but here’s the TL;DR version. Apple’s Touch implementation is so good, it can replace the trackpad as your regular input device. Apple didn’t half-ass it here. The company made thoughtful decisions about how the interface should respond to touch, and the result is responsive and reliable. There are a few quirks, but nothing that stops you in your tracks, and you can always retreat to the trackpad.
Touch worked with all the Apple apps and third-party software I tried, but it didn’t work on some games. For example, Resident Evil Village and Total War: Warhammer III do not let you use Touch, and I suspect this is the case for a lot of games that originated on Windows and implement their own maps for input. You probably wouldn’t want to use Touch during gameplay, but it would be convenient when starting a game and navigating its setup screens and settings. Unfortunately, Touch doesn’t work in those situations, either.

				
					

				
			
The touchscreen supports Multi-Touch gestures, which can be modified in a new Touch Display section of System Settings.

Apple




While Apple has done a good job with its first Touch implementation, it’s not a spotlight feature–Touch isn’t even in the name of this new MacBook. I’d go so far as to say that the laptop just happens to have Touch. Apple hasn’t done anything here that requires Touch, so you can buy it, never use Touch, and you won’t miss out on anything. But if Touch is the main reason why you’re considering this laptop, you’ll find it a satisfying implementation, and Apple has gone on record saying it is committed to its development.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Design
Apple took this opportunity to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lighter and a little smaller. Below is a comparison of the dimensions for the 16-inch MacBook Pro models in Apple’s current lineup.


Dimension16″ MacBook Pro
with PROLED XDR Display

Height0.63 in (1.60 cm)0.66 in (1.68 cm)
Width14.0 in (35.55 cm)14.01 in (35.57 cm)
Depth9.62 in (24.42 cm)9.77 in (24.81 cm)
Weight4.1 lb (1.86 kg)4.7 lb (2.15 kg)

 



The size difference between the two laptops is inconsequential overall. The feet are slightly recessed as well, so it rests closer to the table and a smidge lower than the standard model, so you’ll get a bit more wiggle room in tight spaces. 

				
					

				
			
The mini-LED backlit MacBook Pro with an aluminum logo is a bit taller than the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




On the other hand, the weight difference is huge. The PROLED XDR Display laptop is 12 percent lighter than the standard MacBook Pro, and that’s noticeable when carrying it around on a bus commute. The laptop’s shell retains the same general design as before, in the same two colors Space Black and Silver. However, the corners of the display are a bit more rounded than before and now the bottom of the display is rounded as well. Also the hinge has been adjusted to better accommodate taps and swipes.
However, since you’ll want people to know you’re using one of these laptops, Apple added a bit of flourish to the back by replacing the shiny aluminum Apple logo with one that glows. It’s a callback to the era when the Mac laptops had the glowing Apple logo from 1999 to 2015. No other MacBook has it, and with its placement on Apple’s most expensive and extravagant laptop, the glowing Apple is now a status symbol. 
As with the older implementations, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen’s brightness. Turn up the screen, and the logo brightens; turn down the screen, and the logo dims. If you want to turn it off completely, you need to use a Terminal command, as detailed in an Apple support document–odd that it’s not an option in System Settings.

				
					

				
			
The glowing Apple logo on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (right) used to be on older laptops, such as the 2010 MacBook Pro (left).

Roman Loyola/Foundry




PROLED MacBook Pro: Dynamic Island
Did you hate the notch at the top of Apple’s MacBook displays? It’s gone! Rejoice! But it’s not forgotten, because there’s still a camera hole at the top of the display. Apple opted to cut an opening for the FaceTime camera rather than place it under the display as it does with the iPhone Duo‘s inside display. Considering how poor we found the Duo camera’s image quality is, sticking with a cutout (and a smaller one at that) is the right choice. One small side effect: The new camera cutout is slightly lower than the notch was, so it means the menu bar is a little deeper.
Instead of simply replacing the notch with a static pill-shaped cutout, Apple has brought the Dynamic Island to macOS, displaying notifications, Spotlight search, Siri AI, Live Activities, and more. It works as it does on the iPhone. I’m glad it’s on the Mac, but it did take some adjustment, because these elements are now at the top center of the display, whereas before they either popped up in the middle of the display or off to the right. 

				
					

				
			
The notch is gone on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. A less distracting, iPhone-like pillbox replaces it.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




An important thing to know is that Live Activities isn’t a feature that’s only for Dynamic Island. In the macOS 27.3 beta, the feature works on other Macs, appearing as a small oval in the menu bar. But it’s much more elegant here.
The FaceTime camera has CenterStage, like the standard MacBook Pro. But it also has advanced video stabilization, which you won’t find on any other MacBook. I’m not sure how crucial this feature is, since I don’t typically move my laptop around while using the camera. But since this laptop is targeted at content creation, it’s a feature Apple felt was necessary.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Performance
New laptop, new chip, right? Nope. Apple is using the M5 Pro or M5 Max for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the same chips that were released in the MacBook Pro earlier this year. This decision stems from changes to Apple’s chip development plans in response to growing demand for AI processing. However, the chip series Apple decided to fast-track, the M7, isn’t ready, so M5 chips it is.
The M5 Max is impressive, and fortunately, the major new component of the laptop, the OLED, doesn’t affect chip performance. So, across the board, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and the standard model offer the same speed.

		
			


If you want the fastest MacBook Pro, it’s the one with the M5 Max chip and the 40-core GPU, tested here. The M5 Max is 26 percent faster than the M4 Max and 45 percent faster than the M3 Max in Geekbench’s Multi-Core CPU benchmark. Geekbench checks the overall CPU performance.

		
			


Cinebench is a benchmark tool that uses Maxon’s Redshift render engine, so it’s a good gauge for professionals who handle content. The M5 Max is 18 percent faster than the M4 Max, and 38 percent faster than an M3 Max.

		
			


The difference between the M5 Max and M4 Max here isn’t noticeable. They both rely on the built-in encoder on each chip, and Apple didn’t make many changes between the two chips.

		
			


A 4K iMovie video export at the High setting was 14 percent faster on the M5 Max than on the M4 Max. With the export set to Best (ProRes), there’s no difference.

		
			


Apple introduced major SSD speed improvements with the MacBook Pro earlier this year, and they’re in this new laptop, too. Interestingly, the PROLED laptop’s read speed is noticeably faster than what we’ve seen previously.

		
			


You know what looks really nice? Video games on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. While there are gaming PC laptops, Apple’s new laptop doesn’t really compete with them, since those devices optimize for video performance. Apple’s laptop performs well, but Windows has a distinct advantage when it comes to the available game library.

		
			

		
		

		
			


The M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display mirrors the results of the M5 Max Mac Studio in Geekbench’s AI tests. If you’re an AI developer, it’s nice to know that you won’t lose performance while using a laptop.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Battery life
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has the same 99.6-watt-hour battery as its mini-LED backlit companion. Thus, both laptops with the M5 Max chip have the same rating of 22 hours of video streaming and 16 hours of wireless web use.
Our test for battery life involves saving a video to the SSD and then running it on a continuous loop until the battery runs out. With the display set to 150 nits, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasted about 24 hours, the same as the 15-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with mini-LED.

				
					

				
			
Apple has not changed the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s ports. Pictured here: MagSafe, two Thunderbolt 5/USB ports, audio jack.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Apple has not commented on whether OLED uses more power than mini-LED. Since OLED technology switches off to display black, it could conceivably use less power, since the backlight with mini-LED is always on, even with black. On the other hand, OLED gets much brighter than mini-LED, so it can use more power in high-brightness situations. With this in mind, macOS’s dark mode could help this laptop save energy (plus it looks great).
The same stuff
In addition to the chip options, there is a lot more about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that’s the same as the standard MacBook Pro. Here’s a quick summary of the features that are the same.
Ports: three Thunderbolt 5/USB 4 ports, an HDMI port, a MagSafe connector, an SDXC Card slot, and a 3.5mm audio jack. If you want more details on the ports, you can read our M4 Pro MacBook Pro review.
External displays: With the M5 Max, the PROLED MacBook Pro supports up to four displays at native resolutions of 6K at 60Hz or 4K at 144Hz. It can also display two screens at up to a native resolution of 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz, or 4K at 240Hz.
Wireless connectivity: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), Bluetooth 6, and Thread.
Speakers: six-speaker sound system with force-canceling woofers.
Backlit Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and Magic Trackpad.

				
					

				
			
An SDXC Card slot, Thunderbolt 5/USB, and HDMI.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Should you buy the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display?
Gawd, I love the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. I’m excited every time I use it. The OLED display is a revelation. Touch is intriguing and sometimes fun. The performance is satisfying. The lighter weight and smaller design are a welcome relief. The pill-shaped camera cutout is much less of a visual detraction than the notch, and the Dynamic Island is useful. It’s a laptop that gets everything right.
If you can afford it, I recommend the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display to anyone. No matter what kind of work you do, you should use the best tools available, right? That’s this MacBook. The reality, however, is that everything is more expensive than it’s ever been. We all need to take a deeper consideration of costs, so here’s more specific advice.
If you are a professional whose work depends on visual integrity, this laptop is a vital tool. The OLED display will help you excel at what you do. It’s worth the investment, and you’ll find it will pay for itself in no time.
For other professionals whose work isn’t graphically dependent, the M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro with the mini-LED backlit display is more than capable of meeting your needs. The display has always been great and doesn’t disappoint. It offers the same chip performance as the PROLED model, the same external display support, the same ports, and the same speakers. If you don’t need or really want the OLED display, there’s no need to pay for it. But you’ll still be happy that you did.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display raises the bar for Apple excellence. It’s a landmark addition to the Mac lineup, and a reminder of what makes users devoted to the Mac. Customers now have plenty of laptop choices, with the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It’s a good time to be a Mac user.

title: Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger review: An Apple charging station with room for iPad
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating

Fast Watch Charger

Cons

USB-C drops to 18W during wireless charging
Our Verdict 
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is a tidy charging stand that will clear your desk from straggling cables, wirelessly for the iPhone, Watch, and AirPods, plus an iPad or even MacBook via a wired connection. You can buy cheaper and faster charging stands, but the neat iPad support helps this one stand out. Just remember that the USB-C output drops to 18W when wireless charging is also in use.

What is it? A charging stand that wirelessly charges iPhone, AirPods and Apple Watch, and hosts a charging port for an iPad or MacBook.
Who is it best for? iPad users who want to charge all their Apple devices at the same time.
Who should skip it? If you don’t have an iPad, you’ll be better off with a 3-in-1 or even 2-in-1 (if you don’t have an Apple Watch) wireless charger.
There are many 2-in-1 wireless charging stands (iPhone and AirPods) and 3-in-1 (iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch) magnetic multi marvels, and we’ve tested a large selection of them in our best wireless iPhone charger roundup.
If you want to charge your iPad at the same time as all the above Apple devices, you’ll generally need a second cable from the wall or even two chargers.
3-in-1 magnetic wireless chargers can hoist even the iPhone Pro Max aloft but most would buckle and fall over if you introduced even an iPad mini into the action. The iPad requires a different charging connection, so we’ll stop a moment to explain the options.
How do you wirelessly charge an iPad?
As it doesn’t come with built-in MagSafe charging coils, you can’t simply place an iPad on wireless chargers like you do with an iPhone. The closest you’ll get is the Kuxiu M30 magnetic smart connector charger that brings a MagSafe-like charging experience to compatible iPads by snapping magnetically to the back of the tablet and drawing power through a 3-pogo-pin Smart Connector. Because iPads with these pins have them in different configurations, you need a size-specific charger for select iPad Pro and iPad Air models—it’s a neat solution but nowhere near as convenient as MagSafe/Qi2.
There are several reasons why iPads don’t do MagSafe. iPads have larger batteries than iPhones (19-40Wh vs 12-20Wh), and these generate too much heat to be safe if charged wirelessly. Also, most iPads use aluminum on their back shells compared to iPhone’s glass, and this interferes with the magnetic fields used in wireless charging.

				
					

				
			The Zens 4-in-1 is a neat stand with charging points for iPhone (raised and ready for StandBy Mode), Apple Watch (supporting Nightstand Mode), AirPods (on the other side to the Watch charger), and a bar to rest your iPad when charging via the side USB-C port.
Simon Jary




Zens offers a simple 4-in-1 solution
The Zens 4-1 Wireless Charger looks like a standard sleek 3-in-1 iPhone charging stand made from zinc alloy but has a bar at the back to prop up an iPad, with a powerful USB-C port on one side to connect it.
It’s a good-looking stand, with Apple’s badge of approval as it is one of few available at the Apple Store.
At the front there’s an elevated iPhone charging pad that’s tilt-adjustable up and down, but not side to side. This is a Qi2 charger and so maxes power output to the iPhone at 15W rather than the latest and greatest 25W Qi2.2. The difference is about 15 minutes (45 vs 30 minutes) in the time it takes to wirelessly charge an iPhone from 0-50%. Compatible newer iPhones can charge faster with a suitable higher-powered wireless charger, but if you charge your devices overnight, the Zens stand’s 15W limit shouldn’t bother you.

				
					

				
			You can flatten the Watch charger when not in use.
Simon Jary




The pop-up Apple Watch module on the Zens 4-1 Wireless Charger can be charged at a rapid 7.5W, faster than most 5W Watch chargers that are able to claim Apple’s official “Fast Charge” status. The AirPods charge at up to 5W, which is as much power as they can take on board, so you won’t get faster.

				
					

				
			The Zens 4-in-1 ships with a 12-inch cable to connect the iPad. It will serve a MacBook too, but you can’t squeeze the laptop into the same space as the iPad slips into.
Simon Jary




At the side is the USB-C port for attaching your iPad, or a second iPhone or any USB-C charged device via the included 12-inch (300mm) cable. It’s rated at up to 60W when used alone, which is enough to charge an iPad or a compatible MacBook. Indeed, it’s enough to fast-charge an iPad—if you’re not charging anything else at the same time. Everyone’s in a hurry sometimes, and if you want to power-up your iPhone as fast as possible use the port and cable for faster wired charging when the wireless charging modules aren’t in use. You’ll need a Lightning cable if your phone is older than an iPhone 15. If you want to connect your MacBook further away, look for a longer USB-C cable.
The Zens 4-in-1 ships with a 65W wall charger (and 5ft/1.5m cable), so you’ll need to share that amount of power around the devices when charging several at the same time. It’s not a USB-C wall charger so is proprietary to the Zens charger.
Note that, as with most multi-device chargers, power output is reduced when charging several devices simultaneously. The USB-C port’s maximum output drops from 60W to 18W when wireless charging is also in use—enough to charge an iPad, although more slowly than when the port is used alone. For a MacBook, whether it can maintain the battery level will depend on the model and workload.
Handily, the Zens 4-in-1 also comes with interchangeable plugs for US (Type A), UK (Type G), and EU (Type C). That doesn’t make it a convenient travel charger, mind you—it’s relatively compact at 6.9 x 5.9 x 4.3 inches (175 x 150 x 110mm) but not one you’ll likely slip into your backpack. It also weighs 23 oz (650g). In comparison, the more travel-friendly Mous 3-In-1 Wireless Portable Charger weighs 85g, although it’s painfully slow at 7.5W.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




How much does the Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger cost?
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is priced at $159.99 / £159.99, although you’ll find it a little cheaper on the Apple Store ($149.95 / £149.95) and maybe Amazon depending on your timing.
You can certainly buy cheaper charging stations but few with the ability to charge a fourth device at the same time. One alternative is Mophie’s 4-in-1 StealthCharge Wireless Charge Stand ($179.95 / £139.95), which has a smaller footprint and 25W iPhone charging—although while it can charge a fourth device via its integrated retractable cable, it lacks the Zens charger’s neat iPad stand bar.
Should you buy the Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger?
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is a tidy white/silver charging stand that will reduce cable clutter on your desk for up to four of your devices, wirelessly for the iPhone, Watch and AirPods, plus an iPad or even MacBook via a wired connection. You can buy cheaper and faster charging stands, but the neat iPad support helps this one stand out. Just remember that the USB-C output drops to 18W when wireless charging is also in use.

title: Pro-privacy Apple could end up as a Trojan Horse for surveillance tech
content:
Macworld





Two of the things I dislike most about modern life are AI and surveillance. So naturally, I was pretty jazzed in September when Apple announced Siri Recap and Live Rewind, two new AI-powered surveillance features coming to the Apple Watch Series 12. Ain’t that just a kick in the head, I thought.
But I was wrong. Or, at least, overreacting a little. As sinister listening technologies go, the Audio Intelligence features are pretty harmless.
Live Rewind, for example, has very clearly been designed from the ground up with privacy in mind, to the extent that its usefulness is frequently limited by such considerations. The tiny 15-second listening window, the limited physical range, the lack of speaker attribution, the inability to screenshot transcripts: all mildly annoying for good-faith users, and devastating for bad actors and eavesdroppers. Yes, these features listen in on you and the people around you. But they do so in the most privacy-friendly way you can imagine.
Apple has long marketed itself as the pro-privacy tech company, but the privacy measures in Audio Intelligence are hardcore even by its standards. (Live Rewind would be a lot more useful if its maker embraced the creepy tech vibe. I’m not saying Apple should have done that; I’m just pointing it out.) And there’s a good reason for Apple’s overabundance of caution: as a general rule, normal people despise listening tech, and the company doesn’t want that kind of controversy.
We’ve been here before, you see. Any technology that’s perceived as listening in on us without informed consent is liable to stir up a passionate response.
Take Google Glass. Google launched its range of smart glasses back in 2012, and their ability to semi-covertly record audio and video of passers-by made them so unpopular that wearers were called “Glassholes” and, in a few cases, were physically assaulted. Then in 2013 the launch of the Xbox One was overshadowed by privacy concerns after it emerged that the device’s Kinect peripheral could monitor users’ conversations; Microsoft was obliged to reverse a previously announced policy that the Kinect had to be plugged in at all times.
Paranoid or not, many tech users suspect that the digital voice assistants in our phones and smart speakers record what we say at all times, despite makers’ insistence that this only happens when the trigger phrase is uttered. Fairly obviously, some form of listening is necessary for the trigger phrase to be recognised, but the theory is that any other audio that’s heard is promptly discarded. Except when it’s not. “I felt invaded,” said one Alexa user whose private conversation was recorded and sent to a random number in her address book. “A total privacy invasion.”
Perhaps we’d expect that kind of thing from Amazon, whose business model relies on extensive data about potential customers. But even Apple has been caught with its hand in the data jar. A class-action lawsuit filed in 2019 alleged that Siri had listened in on users’ conversations and then shared the results with advertisers. Apple denied any wrongdoing but last year settled for $95m.
Considering public distrust of surveillance technology and anger against private individuals who enable it, we can hardly be surprised that Apple is treading so lightly in the execution of its Audio Intelligence features. It doesn’t want to be perceived as spying on its users, and it doesn’t want Apple Watch owners to be attacked. (I don’t want that either, to be clear.) The privacy measures in Audio Intelligence are as thoughtful as they are predictable, and I think they will be accepted in good faith.
But here’s my worry. Apple is very good at leading cultural shifts, either through marketing clout or its ability to absorb the hits and keep fighting. It dropped the headphone port from the iPhone in 2016, a time when such a move seemed unthinkable. Everyone complained, then it became the new normal and other companies followed suit. Apple performed a similar trick by removing the bundled earbuds and charger from iPhone boxes in 2020, which too became accepted in time. It kickstarted the popularity of MP3 players, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and wireless earbuds simply by entering those markets, and the launch of the iPhone Duo is widely expected to send foldables into the mainstream.
So what happens if Apple does something similar with eavesdropping tech? Can the company launder the reputation of this singularly hated branch of technology? Can it get people to accept the idea that the things they say are constantly being recorded and fed into AI models?
Other companies will be watching the progress of Live Rewind and Siri Recap with great interest. The execution of these features strikes me as intentional, considered, and ethical. But the fundamental idea is still an unpalatable one: They listen in without explicit consent, and they record in some way what they hear. That remains, for the time being, an idea that would struggle to gain mainstream acceptance. 
But Apple may be about to help it achieve that. And that’s when it becomes a lot easier for other applications to build a user base. Applications that care a lot less about privacy, and a lot more about grabbing data. Ain’t that just a kick in the head.

				
					

				
			
Foundry

title: macOS versions in order: Complete Mac OS X and macOS history
content:
Macworld





Since the debut of Mac OS X in 2001, Apple has released dozens of versions of its Mac operating system, introducing new features, design updates, performance improvements, and more. From early big-cat releases such as Panther and Leopard to more recent California-inspired versions like Sonoma, Sequoia, Tahoe and Golden Gate, each release marked a new chapter in the Mac’s evolution.
Whether you’re trying to identify the version running on your Mac, check compatibility before upgrading, or find out which releases are still supported, this guide covers every Mac OS X and macOS version in chronological order – from the original Mac OS X Cheetah to macOS 27 Golden Gate. 
Discover the major features introduced with each release, including Spotlight in Tiger, Time Machine in Leopard, Siri in Sierra and the enhanced Spotlight search introduced in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
Below, you’ll find a complete list of macOS versions in order, along with release dates, codenames, key details and support information.


What is the latest macOS version? 
macOS 27 Golden Gate was released on September 14, 2026, but the latest version is macOS 27.2, which was released on October 26, 2026 and improved Siri’s memory and use of personal context, added conversation-based suggestions in Messages and enhanced Shared Albums, alongside bug fixes and security updates. 
Apple will continue to update Golden Gate with new features throughout 2026 and 2027.
For details of the latest macOS 27 release, new features, beta updates and compatibility, see our complete macOS 27 Golden Gate Guide.






macOS version history: Every macOS and Mac OS X version and the features it brought 
macOS is Apple’s operating system for the Mac, in the same way iOS runs on the iPhone and iPadOS runs on the iPad. It provides the user interface and acts as the link between a Mac’s hardware and its software.
All Macs have run macOS – formerly known as Mac OS X – since its debut in 2001. Before that, Apple computers used Mac OS 9. macOS is based on Unix technology developed at NeXT, the company Steve Jobs founded before returning to Apple.
Since its launch on March 24, 2001, macOS has evolved significantly, gaining tighter integration with iOS devices, cloud services, and productivity features such as Time Machine, Quick Look, Exposé, Spaces, and Desktop Stacks.
Below is a complete overview of macOS versions, showing how Apple’s desktop operating system has developed over time, along with the official names and internal codenames used for each release.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




OS X 10 beta: Released in September 13, 2000, this preview version of OS X was codenamed Kodiak. It was based on technology from NeXT Computer, which was another company founded by Apple founder Steve Jobs and it introduced the Aqua user interface as well as protected memory and preemptive multitasking to stop crashes. This beta cost $29.95.
OS X 10.0: Code named Cheetah, this was the first major release of Mac OS X, arriving on March 14, 2001. It was Apple’s first OS built on a Unix-based foundation. Unfortunately it was slow and rough around the edges.
OS X 10.1: Just a few months ofter the first version of Mac OS X launched, Apple introduced the Puma update on September 15, 2001. This time is was stable and ready for everyday use, hardware support was better, and other issues with the fist version were addressed. 
OS X 10.2: Jaguar arrived on August 14, 2002, significantly improving performance and usability, introducing Quartz Extreme for smoother graphics, a faster Finder, and better networking. iChat was one of the new features. 
OS X 10.3: In October 2003 Apple introduced Panther which focused on speed, stability, and polish, delivering noticeably faster performance and a more responsive system. New features included: Exposé for managing windows, Fast User Switching, and FileVault disk encryption. Safari arrived as the default web browser.
OS X 10.4: Tiger arrived in April 2005 with new features like Spotlight search and Dashboard widgets. 
OS X 10.5: In October 2007 Leopard arrived and added features like Time Machine for automated backups, Spaces for virtual desktops, and a redesigned Finder with Cover Flow. Time Machine also arrived as a simple way to back up a Mac. 
OS X 10.6: Released in 2009, Snow Leopard focused on performance, stability, and efficiency rather than flashy new features.
OS X 10.7 Lion: Arriving in July 2011, Lion brought iPad-inspired features to the Mac, like Launchpad, full-screen apps, and multi-touch gestures. It also introduced system-wide Auto Save, Resume, and Versions so that users didn’t need to worry about manual saving. 
OS X 10.8: A year later, in 2012 Mountain Lion brought more iOS features to the Mac including Messages, Reminders, Notes, Notification Center, and iCloud integration. Gatekeeper security was also emphasised. 

				
					

				
			The Notification Center made its debut in OS X Mavericks.
Foundry




OS X 10.9: In October 2013 Apple stopped naming Mac OS X versions after big cats and switched to Californian landmarks, starting with Mavericks. It introduced features like Finder Tabs, Tags, and memory compression, making Macs faster and more responsive. It was also the first time Apple offered the Max OS X update for free. 
OS X 10.10: Introduced in October 2014, Yosemite brought a major visual redesign with a cleaner, flatter interface, translucent elements, and a more modern look inspired by iOS (iOS 7 with its big redesign had been introduced in 2013). Continuity features from the iPhone and iPad included Handoff, iCloud Drive, and the ability to make and receive calls and texts from a Mac. 
OS X 10.11: El Capitan arrived in September 2015 and, like Snow Leopard in 2007, focused more on refinement and stability. It brought improvements like better window management (Split View), smoother graphics, and performance boosts.
macOS 10.12: In September 2016 macOS Sierra was the first version to be referred to as macOS rather than Mac OS X, better aligning it with iOS, watchOS and tvOS. It brought Siri to the Mac and improved integration with iPhone and iPad with features like Universal Clipboard. 
macOS 10.13: This was another update where the focus was on performance rather than flashy new features. High Sierra in September 2017 brought updates to core apps like Photos and Safari but mostly focused on security and efficiency updates.
macOS 10.14: In September 2018, Mojave introduced a system-wide Dark Mode and introduced Desktop Stacks for better file organization. 

				
					

				
			Dark Mode debuted in Mojave.
Foundry




macOS 10.15: Arriving in October 2019, Catalina replaced iTunes with separate Music, TV, and Podcasts apps and introduced Sidecar so an iPad could be used as a second display for a Mac. It also ended support for 32-bit apps.
macOS 11: Big Sur was the first version to drop the ten, from Mac OS X, and start again at 11. Launched in November 2020 it was a major redesign of Apple’s Mac operating system, with a cleaner, more modern interface, updated icons, a refined Control Center, and closer visual alignment with iOS.
macOS 12: Arriving in October 2021, Monterey introduced Universal Control (one mouse/keyboard across Mac and iPad) and improved FaceTime.
macOS 13: macOS Ventura arrived in October 2022 and introduced Stage Manager for better multitasking, improved Continuity features (including using an iPhone as a webcam, and brought major updates to Mail, Safari, and Spotlight. Read: How Ventura and Monterey compare. 
macOS 14: In September 2023 Sonoma made the desktop more immersive with animated wallpapers and desktop widgets you can interact with. There were game-focused improvements in Game Mode and video conferencing features like Presenter Overlay were added. Here’s how Sonoma compares to Ventura. 
macOS 15: A year later in September 2024, Sequoia brought iPhone Mirroring and added Apple Intelligence features. Here’s how Sequoia compares to Sonoma. 
macOS 26: Tahoe arrived in September 2025 with a bold new Liquid Glass design with transparent, customizable interface elements and tighter integration with iPhone and iPad. As with iPhone and iPad, Apple unified version numbering, so the macOS jumped from macOS 15 to 26. Apple also expanded Apple Intelligence, improved Spotlight, improved the Phone related features, and added a new Games app. This was the final macOS version to support Intel-based Macs. See how macOS 26 Tahoe compares to macOS 15 Sequoia.
macOS 27: macOS 27 Golden Gate was released on September 14, 2026, bringing Siri AI, Visual Intelligence, enhanced Spotlight search, performance improvements, and refinements to the Liquid Glass interface introduced with macOS Tahoe. Golden Gate is also the first major macOS release to require Apple silicon, ending support for Intel-powered Macs. See how macOS 27 Golden Gate compares to macOS 26 Tahoe.





List of macOS versions and latest versions

 FAQ 


1.
Which macOS versions are still supported?
macOS 27 Golden Gate: The current version, receiving new features, bug fixes and security updates.
macOS 26 Tahoe: The previous major version, continuing to receive security updates.
macOS 15 Sequoia: Also continuing to receive security updates.
Apple released macOS 27.2, macOS 26.7.2 and macOS 15.8.2 on October 26, 2026.
Apple generally issues security updates for the current macOS release and the previous two major versions, but this pattern should not be treated as a guaranteed support period.
macOS Sonoma appears to have left the regular update cycle; its most recent update was macOS 14.8.9 on August 6, 2026. Older versions can occasionally receive exceptional fixes, but those releases do not indicate ongoing regular support.
See: How long do Macs and MacBooks last? We also have a full list of which Macs run which versions of macOS here.





2.
How does Apple choose Mac OS X and macOS names?
As you can see from the list above, with the exception of the first OS X beta, all versions of the Mac operating system from 2001 to 2012 were named after big cats, from Cheetah to Panther to the final release, Mountain Lion. But while the public-facing builds were named after big cats, internally, they were named after wines (aside from OS X 10.6 which had no codename).
Even after Apple switched public-facing code names to places in California back in 2013, it carried on naming them after wines internally until 2014. In 2015, Apple decided to change the theme of internal code names from wines to types of apples. 
In 2016, Apple took the plunge to unify the branding of its operating systems by rebranding Mac OS X to macOS, which sits nicely alongside iOS, tvOS, and watchOS and paved the way for macOS 11, the successor to Mac OS X, which arrived twenty years after the first beta of Mac OS X.
In 2025, Apple decided to sync up the numbering system between all its operating systems, moving from macOS 14 to macOS 26 to better reflect the year. macOS 26 Tahoe lived most its lifetime as the most recent version in the year 2026 before being replaced with macOS 27 in September 2026.





3.
How do I check my macOS version?
You can tell which version of macOS you are running by clicking on the Apple logo in the top left and choosing About This Mac. 
It will clearly show which version of macOS you are running along with the most recent version that your Mac has installed. 
If you are looking for help installing macOS read: How to update macOS and Fixes for Macs that won’t update. We can also help with How to install macOS on an unsupported Mac.





4.
Can I run the macOS beta? 
You can install a beta version of macOS and test new features that haven’t yet launched. If you want to install the latest beta of macOS read about joining Apple’s beta program.





5.
How can I install the latest version of macOS?
Some Macs will be set to update macOS automatically. If you want your Mac to update automatically follow these steps:
Open System Settings.
Click on General. 
Click on Software Update.
Click on the “i” beside Automatic Updates and make sure that Check for updates, Download new updates when available, and Install macOS updates are selected. This way your Mac will automatically update to the latest version. If you would prefer not to have your Mac do this automatically you can deselect these options. 
Read all about how to update your Mac here.





We also have a list of every version of iOS where you can see the latest versions and how long Apple supports iPhones for.
